sens: Great-grandson of Adam, son of Seth
G1800.detail: Enos is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the New Testament, in the genealogy that Luke traces back to Adam. He is the son of Seth and the father of Kenan (according to Genesis 5:9-10). His name means "man" or "mortal" in Hebrew. In the genealogy of Luke 3:38, he represents a key generation of God's people in the antediluvian ages.
G1800.origine: The Hebrew name אֱנוֹשׁ (Enosh) literally means "man" and comes from the root that designates humanity, particularly in its fragility or mortal condition. It is a name that emphasizes the human nature common to all descendants of Adam. The text of Genesis 4:26 notes that in his time people began to call on the Lord by his name, marking a spiritual moment in antediluvian history.
G1800.emploi: Enos appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:38, in the ascending genealogy of Jesus traced by the evangelist Luke back to Adam. This genealogy establishes that Jesus, presented as the "Son of God" at the end of the list, descends from a long chain of faithful ancestors, including Enos in the tenth generation from Adam. The inclusion of Enos underscores the continuity of God's plan through human generations.

sens: To lean in to listen
To give attention to someone
To welcome a word favorably
G1801.detail: 1. The verb first depicts the physical act of leaning in to hear well: one bends down, listens attentively (literally "to put in the ear"). 2. It then designates the attentive listening itself, the action of paying attention to the one speaking: it is to truly open oneself to their words, not just to hear them by chance. This is why Peter in Acts 2:14 calls out to the crowds: "Lend an ear to my words!" — he calls them to serious, focused listening. 3. By extension, "to lend an ear" can mean to welcome favorably, to consent to listen to what deserves attention.
G1801.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "ear" (Greek οὖς, Latin auris) to which a prefix is added that intensifies the action (ἐν-, "in, into"). It literally means "to put something in the ear" or "to make enter through the ear." In Hebrew, the corresponding verb אָזַן ("to listen, to pay attention") shares this same idea of an active, engaged ear. Greek also uses this verb to render שָׁמַע ("to hear, to listen") or יָחַל ("to wait"), showing that biblical listening is always more than mere passive reception.
G1801.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, at the decisive moment when Peter addresses the crowd on the day of Pentecost. He uses this form in the imperative to command the Jews present in Jerusalem to listen attentively. The choice of this verb is not trivial: Peter does not simply ask to be "allowed to speak," but that they show themselves available, receptive to the word he is about to pronounce — that of the good news of the risen Christ. It is a call to engaged and obedient listening.
G1801.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that "listening" to the Word of God is never passive. It is an attitude of voluntary attention, an opening of the heart. When the Bible tells us to "lend an ear" to the Gospel or to the voice of God, it invites us to go beyond mere physical hearing to enter into conscious and willing obedience. It is a call to truly pay attention, to receive the word with all our being.

sens: Antediluvian patriarch, father of Methuselah
Man taken up to heaven without experiencing death
Figure of faith and pleasing to God
Prophet who announced divine judgment
G1802.detail:
1. Enoch is a patriarch from the antediluvian time, belonging to the lineage from Adam to Noah. He appears in the genealogy of Jesus as the father of Methuselah (Luke 3:37).
2. The remarkable event that characterizes him is his being taken up by God without experiencing physical death: he simply disappeared from the earth because God took him to Himself (Hebrews 11:5). Before this taking up, he had received the testimony of being pleasing to God.
3. The Epistle to the Hebrews cites him as a model of faith: his walk with God and his miraculous taking up show that faith receives divine approval.
4. The book of Jude presents him as a prophet, the seventh from Adam, who prophesied about the coming of the Lord and His judgment (Jude 1:14).
G1802.origine: The Hebrew name חֲנוֹךְ (Hanokh) literally means "initiated" or "educated" — an image of consecration or training. This name perfectly fits the biblical character, who distinguished himself by his intimate relationship with God and exceptional piety. He is one of the few men in the Bible to have been taken directly to heaven.
G1802.emploi: Enoch appears three times in the New Testament. In the Gospel of Luke (3:37), he simply appears in the genealogy of Jesus as an ancestor of the messianic line. The Epistle to the Hebrews (11:5) highlights him as a classic testimony of antediluvian faith: his ability to please God despite the circumstances of his time demonstrates that faith, long before the Law, was already the condition for divine approval. The Epistle of Jude (1:14) identifies him as a prophet and cites his words of judgment against the ungodly, showing that Christian tradition recognizes him with particular prophetic authority.
G1802.portee: Enoch encourages the believer on two levels. First, his life teaches that walking with God — that is, living in communion with Him — is possible and pleasing in His eyes, long before the complete revelation of Christ. Second, his taking up reminds us that God honors those who sincerely seek Him: they receive not only His present approval but a special destiny, escaping ordinary death. For a Christian, this evokes the promise of the rapture of the Church.

sens: The number 6, base number of the numeral system
Duration of six units (days, months, years)
Quantity of six objects or people
G1803.detail:
1. Six is the whole number that follows five. It is a simple counting number used to enumerate or measure: "Now there were six stone jars there for the Jewish rites of purification" (John 2:6).

2. Six often adds to other numbers to express a more precise duration. Elijah prayed "for three years and six months" that it would not rain, a terrible drought period (James 5:17). Similarly, Paul "stayed a year and six months" in Corinth to teach (Acts 18:11).

3. In spiritual contexts, the number 6 can take on symbolic significance. Six jars are found at the wedding at Cana (John 2:6), and six days before Passover Jesus arrives in Bethany (John 12:1). Revelation also mentions the number 666, which represents the number of the beast (Revelation 13:18).
G1803.origine: The Greek word ἕξ comes from Indo-European and simply designates the number that follows five. It is a simple and universal number, without particular Hebrew root: it corresponds to the Hebrew numeral שֵׁשׁ (shesh). This number has no complex etymology — it is a basic term in the counting vocabulary of all ancient languages.
G1803.emploi: The word ἕξ appears 13 times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke and John. It can denote a simple quantity (six jars at Cana in John 2:6), a precise duration (three years and six months in Luke 4:25 and James 5:17), or mark a liturgical moment (six days before Passover in John 12:1, six days after the Transfiguration in Matthew 17:1). In Revelation, it acquires symbolic weight when referring to the number 666 (Revelation 13:18). The number remains objective and factual in most historical and narrative contexts.
G1803.portee: The number 6 reminds the reader that biblical events occur in concrete time and space. In particular, the durations of "three years and six months" mark the intensity of God's judgment (the drought in Elijah's time) or the depth of apostolic ministry. The six days before Passover or after the Transfiguration invite us to see how God structures time according to His plan of salvation.

sens: Proclaiming loudly a word, a news, a message
Making publicly known the qualities, virtues, glorious acts of someone
G1804.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of proclaiming, that is to say, to publicly and authoritatively say a word or news — not whispering or in secret, but making it widely known. The prefix "ex-" reinforces the idea of complete disclosure and outward radiance.
2. In biblical usage, it takes on the more precise nuance of celebrating, making known the virtues and glorious acts of a person: in 1 Peter 2:9, Christians are called to "proclaim the virtues" of Him who called them out of darkness into His marvelous light. It is to declare His excellence, to proclaim His greatness so that it may be known by all.
G1804.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "angellō" (to announce) preceded by the prefix "ex-" (out of, outside), which literally means "to announce outside." In ancient Greek, this formation intensifies the idea of an announcement that goes out, spreads, and resounds publicly. In the Greek version of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew word "sāphar," which means to recount, relate, make known — particularly to describe how one enumerates, celebrates the works and virtues of God.
G1804.emploi: This verb is rare in the New Testament: it appears only once in the Segond (1 Peter 2:9). Peter uses it to urge Christians to proclaim, to make known to the world the "virtues" (that is, the wonderful qualities, power, and glory) of Him who saved them. The context shows that this proclamation is not a mere fleeting announcement, but the living manifestation of the transformation that faith in Jesus brings: from darkness to light. It is a call for the believer's entire life to proclaim the greatness of Christ.
G1804.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand his mission: it is not just about talking about Jesus, but about proclaiming His glory — making Him known as someone great, worthy, and alive — through words and through all of life. The believer becomes the public herald of Christ's virtues, displaying His beauty and power to a world in need.

sens: To free someone from slavery or condemnation by paying the price
To fully take advantage of an opportunity, a fleeting moment
G1805.detail:
1. To redeem primarily means to free someone who is under the power of another by paying a ransom. It is the act of one who pulls someone out of slavery or condemnation. For Paul, this is exactly what Christ did for us: He paid the ultimate price to deliver us from the curse of the law and our bondage to sin (Galatians 3:13 and 4:5). The word evokes a transaction where the price paid secures freedom.
2. To redeem also means to fully seize something that will last only a moment — to make the most of every opportunity before it disappears. When Paul exhorts the Ephesians and Colossians to "redeem the time," he calls them to make the best use of every moment, for the days are evil and the opportunity may never return (Ephesians 5:16, Colossians 4:5).
G1805.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "agorazô" (to buy) preceded by the prefix "ex" which intensifies the action. This combination suggests the idea of buying completely, taking possession for oneself by paying the price. It is a commercial term that has become metaphorical: in the biblical world, slaves were redeemed by paying the necessary sum. Paul uses this marketplace vocabulary to express the spiritual reality of our liberation in Christ — it came at a real cost, paid by Jesus Himself.
G1805.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in Paul's writings. Twice it expresses spiritual redemption: Christ redeems believers from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13) and frees those who were enslaved to the law to give them divine adoption (Galatians 4:5). Twice he urges believers to redeem the present time, that is, to make good use of it in the face of the world's hostility (Ephesians 5:16, Colossians 4:5). The meaning shifts from the price paid by Christ to the vigilance we must have over every moment of our lives.
G1805.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that our freedom cost infinitely dear — it is the fruit of Jesus' redemptive work. But it also urges us to live accordingly: if we have been redeemed, we must not waste our present time. To redeem the time means to live consciously, wisely, taking into account the brevity of life and the eternal stakes.

sens: To bring someone out of a place, to lead them outside
To free someone by making them leave a place where they were held
To lead a group, a multitude out of a territory or situation
To let go, to set free
G1806.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to lead someone outside, to bring them out of a closed place or territory. Mark 15:20 describes the soldiers who "led" Jesus to His execution, pulling Him from the praetorium. John 10:3 speaks of the shepherd who "leads out" his sheep from the fold. It is a direct action, a movement outward.
2. To free someone who was locked up or held: in Acts 12:17, the angel "brought" Peter out of his cell, miraculously delivering him. The word evokes here the breaking of captivity, an escape or deliverance.
3. To lead an entire people or crowd to a new destination: in Acts 7:36, Moses "led out" an entire multitude from Egypt, bringing them to freedom. It is an exodus, an organized departure of a mass of people. The emphasis is on leadership and the collective project.
4. To set free, to grant freedom to someone: in Acts 16:37, Paul demands that the magistrates come themselves to set them in "freedom," not to secretly drive them away like prisoners. The word here designates the official act of releasing someone.
G1806.origine: The word combines the prefix "ἐξ" (ex-, out, outside) and the verb "ἄγω" (to lead, to bring). It literally means "to lead out." In Hebrew, it regularly translates the verb יָצָא (yatsa) in the causative form, which means "to bring out." The Greek word captures the image of an action that extracts someone from a place and places them outside, hence the family of the verb "ἄγω" (leader, conductor in French). This construction clearly shows the directed and voluntary nature of the action.
G1806.emploi: This verb appears 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Acts and the Gospels. It is used in very varied contexts: execution (Mark 15:20), guiding sheep (John 10:3), miraculous deliverance (Acts 5:19; 12:17), historical exodus (Acts 7:36), and orders of expulsion (Acts 16:37-39; 21:38). The context changes the emphasis of the meaning: sometimes it is the action of leading, sometimes liberation, sometimes expulsion. In Hebrews 8:9, the verb evokes the new covenant, recalling how God had once "led out" Israel from Egypt. The usage converges on an idea of transition, of moving from one state to another.
G1806.portee: This word speaks to the believer of deliverance and divine leadership. When the Bible says that God "leads out" His people, it announces a real liberation, not a mere vague promise. Peter pulled from prison, Israel brought out of Egypt: these are concrete acts that testify that God is capable of breaking chains. For the disciple, it is an assurance that God can pull us from all that holds us captive — sin, fear, slavery — and lead us to the freedom He has promised.

sens: to remove something forcefully or vigorously
to take something out of a situation or danger
to deliver someone from danger or oppression
to choose, select for oneself
G1807.detail:
1. To tear away means to remove something quickly and energetically: Jesus invites us to tear out the eye that causes us to stumble, meaning to separate ourselves completely and without hesitation (Matthew 5:29). It is a radical gesture that allows for no compromise.

2. The word can also simply mean to remove something from a place or situation: the Roman centurion takes Paul from the hands of the Jews who were lynching him (Acts 23:27), thus rescuing him from immediate danger.

3. Figuratively, to tear away means to deliver someone from peril, slavery, or oppression. God delivered Joseph from his tribulations in Egypt (Acts 7:10), and He promised to deliver His people from Egyptian slavery (Acts 7:34). It is a powerful and saving intervention.

4. In certain contexts, the word can mean to choose or select for oneself: the Lord chose Paul to bring him out of paganism and into His redeemed people (Acts 26:17, in an alternative reading).
G1807.origine: The Greek word ἐξαιρέω (exaireō) is composed of the prefix ἐξ (ex, "out of") and the verb αἱρέω (haireō, "to take, seize"). The basic image is that of "taking something and removing it" or "pulling something towards oneself." In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew נָצַל (natzal) in the causative form, which carries the idea of "to liberate, save," particularly in contexts of divine intervention in the face of danger. The composition of the word reinforces the idea of a decisive and complete separation.
G1807.emploi: The verb ἐξαιρέω appears 8 times in the New Testament, primarily in Acts. It is used in three contexts: first, as an image of the radical break with sin (Matthew 5:29 and 18:9, where it refers to tearing out one's eye); secondly, to describe divine intervention in the history of salvation (Acts 7:10, 34, where God delivers His people or His servants); and finally, to recount concrete events: Peter's deliverance from prison by the angel (Acts 12:11), the centurion's intervention who takes Paul from the Jews (Acts 23:27), or the Lord's call that pulled Paul from darkness (Acts 26:17 and Galatians 1:4). The meaning oscillates between physical tearing away and spiritual deliverance, depending on the context.
G1807.portee: This word invites Christians to take seriously the break with sin: it is not merely a matter of moderation, but a radical "tearing away," as Jesus teaches. At the same time, the word assures us that it is God Himself who tears us away from sin and danger: deliverance is not primarily our work, but His saving work in our lives. This dual meaning—our part and God's part—gives the biblical message its full strength.

sens: To take away, to withdraw something from its place
To distance someone from a community
G1808.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to take away or withdraw something from the place where it is—like lifting an object to move it. In 1 Corinthians 5:13, the Apostle Paul uses this verb to express the idea of removing the wicked from among the believers: to take the person out of the community, to keep them away.
2. In this ecclesial context, "to remove" takes on a moral and disciplinary nuance: it involves excluding someone who persists in wrongdoing. It is an act of justice that preserves the purity of the assembly of believers.
G1808.origine: The Greek word is formed from the prefix ἐξ- (ex-, "out of") and the verb αἴρω (airō, "to lift, to raise"). The basic image is therefore that of lifting something out of its place. The word translates several Hebrew verbs in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) that express the idea of removing, withdrawing, or distancing.
G1808.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 5:13. Paul cites the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 17:7, where it is prescribed to remove the wicked from among the people) to justify the disciplinary exclusion of a member of the Corinthian church who commits incest. The word thus applies to a strict and solemn action: the expulsion of the unrepentant sinner from the Christian community, in order to maintain the holiness of the assembly and to protect other believers.
G1808.portee: This passage reminds Christians that love is not synonymous with limitless tolerance. The Church has the duty, as a last resort and with much prayer, to exclude one who refuses to repent of serious and public sins. It is an act of love towards the assembly as well as towards the sinner himself, as it may serve to bring him back to repentance.

sens: To demand insistently, using one's authority
To require for oneself, to have something returned
G1809.detail:
1. The verb evokes a request that is not a mere polite inquiry, but one that comes with a certain authority or force of persuasion. In Luke 22:31, Satan "claims" the disciples: he demands them with determined insistence, almost as a right he would arrogate to himself, with the aim of testing them.
2. More broadly, it means to ask for something for oneself with a clear will to obtain satisfaction. The action implies a certain urgency or firmness in the request, as opposed to a simple submissive prayer.
G1809.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐξ (ex-, "out of," "outside") and the verb αἰτέω (aitéō, "to ask"). This composition reinforces the idea of a demand: it is not an ordinary request, but a demand that is out of the ordinary, made with more weight or authority. This is particularly clear when a person with power or a certain position claims something.
G1809.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:31. It is Jesus speaking to Peter, revealing to him that Satan has "claimed" the disciples to sift them. The context of the passage shows that Satan acts with a sort of authority, making an insistent request to God: he wants to subject the disciples to a trial. The use of "to claim" rather than simple "to ask" or "to pray" emphasizes the determination and assurance with which Satan presents his request.
G1809.portee: This word reminds us that the trials Christians face do not arise by chance: they may be the result of a hostile demand, but they remain under God's sovereignty. Jesus warns His disciples, preparing them for difficulty, not to discourage them, but to strengthen them in trust: it is a word of vigilance and hope.

sens: Without prior warning, in an unexpected manner
Unexpectedly, without transition
Immediately, at that moment
G1810.detail:
1. The word describes what happens unexpectedly, without preparation: in Mark 13:36, Jesus warns his disciples that the master of the house may come "suddenly," when they do not expect it. It conveys the idea of a surprise attack.
2. The word also emphasizes the absence of transition between two states: in Luke 9:39, a spirit seizes the child "immediately," abruptly shifting from calm to crisis. It is the immediacy of the change.
3. In Acts 9:3 and 22:6, it is the bright appearance that strikes Saul "suddenly": the word highlights the sudden brilliance, the irruption of heavenly light. The moment of revelation is marked by a break in ordinary time.
G1810.origine: The word comes from the root meaning "flash" or "bright" (ἄφνω). Its primary image is that of something shining or appearing suddenly — hence the meaning of an arrival or an event that occurs without warning. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates the word פִּתְאוֹם (pitom), which carries the same idea of suddenness, the unexpected that bursts forth.
G1810.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospels and Acts. It describes decisive moments: the arrival of the master (Mark 13:36), the appearance of the heavenly host (Luke 2:13), the attack of the spirit (Luke 9:39), and especially Saul's vision on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3, 22:6). Each time, it marks an event that arises unpredictably and transforms the course of things — an intrusion of the divine or the unexpected into daily reality.
G1810.portee: This word invites the Christian to live in vigilant expectation. Jesus uses it to warn that his return will be unexpected; the believer must not fall asleep spiritually thinking they have time. The other uses (Saul's vision, the appearance of angels) also remind us that God acts according to his plan, not according to our expectations, and that he sometimes intervenes in ways that astonish us — to convert us, guide us, or manifest his glory.

sens: To go after someone or something by taking them as a model or adhering to their teaching
To imitate or reproduce a behavior, practice, or path
To adopt the beliefs or false doctrines of a master
G1811.detail:
1. To follow primarily means to walk after someone or to place oneself under their direction. In 2 Peter 1:16, Paul states that he did not rely on "cleverly devised fables" but on what he had seen, thus refusing to follow the invented accounts of others.
2. The verb also means to adhere to a path, teaching, or practice, making it one's own model. In 2 Peter 2:15, the false prophets "have gone astray by following the way of Balaam," meaning they have reproduced his dishonest conduct motivated by greed.
3. In the context of faith, to follow can refer to the adoption of doctrines or false teachings. In 2 Peter 2:2, "many will follow them in their dissolutions," which means these people will embrace and imitate the false teachings and bad conduct of the seducers.
G1811.origine: The word comes from the Greek prefix ἐξ- (ex-, "out, completely") added to ἀκολουθέω (akoleuthéō, "to follow"). The basic idea is that of movement: to walk behind someone. The compound form with ἐξ- can intensify the meaning, suggesting complete adherence or imitation in every respect. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, there are roots related to the Hebrew verb הלך (halak, "to go, to walk") and פנה (panah, "to turn toward"), which also express the idea of following a direction or model.
G1811.emploi: The verb ἐξακολουθέω appears only three times in the New Testament, all in 2 Peter. Peter uses it to warn readers against false prophets and false doctrines. In 2 Peter 1:16, it refers to refusing to follow fables; in 2 Peter 2:2, it is the threatening action of others who will adopt the lies of false teachers; in 2 Peter 2:15, it is the straying of seducers who imitate Balaam's greed. The context is always one of adherence to a teaching or moral path, whether true or false.
G1811.portee: This verb reminds Christians that to follow means to adopt, reproduce, and integrate into one's life a doctrine or model. For Peter, following false prophets is a real threat: it does not amount to mere passive listening, but to a transformation of conduct. In return, being faithful to the true Gospel means following Christ and his apostles in their authentic teachings. The word calls each person to examine who or what they are truly following.

sens: The number 600, composed of six hundreds
G1812.detail: 1. It is simply the number 600, formed in Greek by the juxtaposition of the numeral adjective "six" and the word "hundreds." It appears twice in Revelation: first in Revelation 13:18, where it is part of the symbolic number of the beast (666 — "six hundred sixty-six"), and then in Revelation 14:20, where it measures in stadia the distance over which the blood is shed during the judgment of the nations ("one thousand six hundred stadia").
G1812.origine: The Greek word ἑξακόσιοι (hexakosioi) is formed from ἕξ (hex, "six") and κόσιοι (kosioi, "hundreds"). It is a compound numeral adjective, following the ordinary structure of compound numbers in Greek. The word has no particular connotation: it is a simple counting instrument.
G1812.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Revelation. In Revelation 13:18, it is part of the enigmatic number 666, which characterizes the beast and which John invites the reader to calculate — it is a number of man, carrying symbolic meaning. In Revelation 14:20, it measures the distance of a valley filled with shed blood, giving an apocalyptic scope to the image of divine judgment. In both cases, the number contributes to the prophetic and visionary dimension of the text.
G1812.portee: These occurrences of the number 600 remind us that Revelation uses numbers not only for counting but to signify spiritual realities. For the Christian reader, this invites discernment in biblical numbers for their symbolic depth, and not to reduce the Word of God to a mere mathematical statement, but to seek the hidden divine message within it.

sens: Remove a trace, a writing by rubbing or washing it away
Sponge, dry by dabbing
Make disappear, annul in a figurative sense
G1813.detail:
1. In the literal and concrete sense, the word refers to the action of rubbing or washing to remove a trace: it is cleaning a surface by rubbing. This is why translators use it to translate the image of 'wiping away' tears (Revelation 7:17: 'God will wipe away every tear from their eyes'), a simple gesture of consolation where the hand makes the tear disappear from the face.

2. In a figurative sense, the word applies to what must completely disappear — a writing, a name, a guilt. In Colossians 2:14, Paul says that Jesus 'erased the certificate that condemned us with its ordinances': the accusation document, the debt note, is annihilated. It is as if a pen passes over a papyrus to make it white and blank.

3. When it comes to sin or the name in the book of life, the word carries a major spiritual significance: what is erased will not return to memory. In Acts 3:19, Peter invites to repentance 'so that your sins may be erased', meaning that God annihilates them in forgetfulness. It is radical forgiveness, absolute new beginning.
G1813.origine: The word is composed of the prefix 'ex-' (out of, completely) and the verb 'aleiphô' (to anoint, to rub, to coat with oil or ointment). The addition of the prefix intensifies the action: it is not simply rubbing, it is rubbing until it disappears. In the Greek Septuagint (translation of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew 'tou'ach' (to smear, to plaster) and also 'mâhâ' (to erase, to make disappear), which shows how the image of physical cleaning extends figuratively to express complete removal.
G1813.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Revelation and in Acts, Colossians. In Revelation 7:17 and 21:4, it depicts future consolation: God will wipe away the tears of those who have suffered, an image of divine tenderness. In Colossians 2:14, Paul uses it to describe the annihilation of the Law that accused us — it is 'erased' by the cross. In Acts 3:19, it is the erasure of sins through repentance and conversion. In Revelation 3:5, the word takes the negative form: Christ will not 'erase' the name of the victor, meaning that this name remains irrevocably inscribed in the book of life. The meaning oscillates between the literal (drying, erasing a writing) and the figurative (annulling, forgiving, comforting).
G1813.portee: This word speaks to the believer two great realities: first, radical forgiveness — God does not erase our sins halfway, debts do not remain halfway, it is a total erasure, as if they had never occurred. Secondly, it is a promise of consolation: in the new heaven, God himself will wipe away our tears, a gesture of infinite tenderness that cancels pain. The term invites the reader to accept the offered forgiveness and to hope for definitive healing.

sens: To project oneself into the air by pushing off the feet with force
A noisy manifestation of joy and freedom
G1814.detail:
1. The verb describes the physical action of jumping, leaving the ground by propelling oneself upward — the movement of a body that leaps vigorously. In Acts 3:8, the lame man from birth, healed by Peter and John in the name of Jesus, 'leaped up' : it is the first time he can perform this simple and natural gesture that was forbidden to him.
2. Beyond the mere movement of the body, the jump becomes the overflowing expression of regained life and joy: this healed man does not merely walk, he 'walks, jumps, and praises God'. His jump shouts his joy of being alive and free, of being transformed. It is the leap of the heart that explodes into visible gestures.
G1814.origine: The Greek word ἐξάλλομαι is composed of the prefix ἐξ (out of, outside) and ἅλλομαι (to jump, to leap). It is the intensive form of jumping, with the idea of bursting out, projecting outward with force. The Hebrew word קָלַל (qalal, literally to become light, quick) conveys a similar meaning. The preposition 'ex' reinforces the idea of an explosion, of energy manifesting outward.
G1814.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 3:8. The context is the miracle of healing: a man who has been lame from birth has just been raised by Peter and John. His jump does not merely describe the physical act of standing up, but the totality of his transformation — he walks, he jumps, he praises God. The jump is the visible and irrepressible sign of a divine power that has restored his bodily integrity and his soul.
G1814.portee: This word teaches that true healing transforms the whole being, body and spirit. The jump of this man is not only the physical proof of the miracle, but the natural overflow of joy and gratitude towards God. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that encountering the power of Christ liberates and makes one rejoice.

sens: Action of rising, returning to life
State of a person returned from the dead
Return to a new life after death
G1815.detail: 1. The word literally describes the action of rising or resurrecting: it is the movement of one who returns to life. The prefix ἐξ reinforces the idea of an exit, an elevation out of the state of death. 2. It also designates the resulting state: being in the resurrection means having left death for a new life. In Philippians 3:11, Paul speaks of 'the resurrection from the dead' to refer to that great event where the dead will rise and enter eternal life with Christ.
G1815.origine: The word is formed from the verb ἐξανίστημι, which means 'to rise by withdrawing' or 'to stand up'. The prefix ἐξ ('out of, outside') intensifies the image: it is truly an exit, an elevation that comes from the outside or above. The family of the word includes ἀνάστασις (simple resurrection), more common in the New Testament. This notion is at the heart of the Christian faith: the risen Christ is its firstborn, and all believers will follow his example.
G1815.emploi: This word appears only once in Philippians 3:11, in the mouth of the apostle Paul. Paul expresses his ardent desire to attain 'the resurrection from the dead' — a rare but powerful language, as it emphasizes the action of rising out of the realm of the dead, rather than the simple condition of living afterward. It is a moment of intimacy where Paul confesses his hope: he hopes to be among those whom Christ will raise at his return.
G1815.portee: This word reminds the believer that resurrection is not an abstraction, but a living action, a power that raises the dead. Paul desires this 'resurrection from the dead', which shows that resurrection is the heart of Christian hope and the prize that a true disciple pursues. It invites the reader to also hope for this new life, not as a distant dream, but as a powerful reality that begins now in the heart of the one who believes in Christ.

sens: Come out of the ground, germinate and grow
Appear, emerge quickly
G1816.detail:
1. This verb describes the seed that comes out of the ground and begins to grow. In Matthew 13:5 and Mark 4:5, the seed that quickly rises on rocky soil illustrates rapid but shallow germination, without deep roots to nourish it.
2. The word more broadly evokes anything that emerges and becomes visible: in the Greek Old Testament, it translates the idea of a plant growing or a light shining and appearing. The image is one of sudden and manifest emergence.
G1816.origine: The word combines three elements: ἐξ (out of), ἀνα (upward) and τέλλω (to cause to rise, shine). This composition reinforces the idea of complete emergence: not only coming out, but coming up, fully manifesting. In the Old Testament, it often translates צָמַח (to grow, to sprout) and זָרַח (to shine, to glow), Hebrew words that evoke the visible appearance of a plant or light.
G1816.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in the same context: the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:5 and Mark 4:5). There, it describes the seed that quickly rises on rocky ground. The common idea is that something hidden suddenly becomes visible and active. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it applies to the growth of plants and the appearance of heavenly light.
G1816.portee: This image of quick rising but without deep roots invites the believer to reflect on the solidity of their own faith. An enthusiastic response to the Word, without rooting in knowledge and life with God, does not bear lasting fruit. The word reminds us that true Christian growth requires solid foundations.

sens: To give birth, to generate offspring
To rise, to stand up
G1817.detail:
1. To raise up offspring means to give birth to children to perpetuate the name of a deceased person. This is the idea of levirate marriage: if a man dies without children, his brother must marry his widow to "raise up offspring for his brother" (Mark 12:19). The word evokes the act of "bringing forth" a new generation from within the family.
2. Intransitively, the word simply means "to rise" or "to stand up": in Acts 15:5, some converted Pharisees "rise up" to speak in the Jerusalem assembly.
G1817.origine: The word comes from the prefix ἐξ ("out of") and the root ἱστημι ("to place, establish, make stand"). It thus evokes the idea of "bringing forth" or "making stand up." In Hebrew, it often translates קוּם (quoum, "to rise, to stand up"), which shares this image of uprightness and establishment. The Greek root is common to verbs like ἵστημι and to nouns like ἐξ-ανάστασις (resurrection).
G1817.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament. In Mark 12:19 and Luke 20:28, Jesus is questioned about the law of levirate marriage: the verb there specifically refers to the obligation to "raise up a descendant" for a deceased person. It is a citation from the Torah explaining levirate marriage (see Deuteronomy 25:5-6). In Acts 15:5, the same verb is used intransitively to say that Pharisees "rise up" to express themselves at the Jerusalem council. The change in meaning (transitive and then intransitive) illustrates the flexibility of this word between the sense of "to give birth" and "to stand up."
G1817.portee: This word reminds us of the heart of the law of levirate marriage: the perpetuation of the name and family heritage, which reflects a deep biblical promise—that of lasting offspring. In Old Testament piety, "being forgotten" (having no offspring) was a curse; "being raised up" by the faithfulness of a relative was a grace. For the Christian reader, this prepares to understand how Jesus himself, as the son of David and heir of the promises, embodies this assurance of life and perpetuity for his people.

sens: To deceive someone by diverting them from the right path through cunning or lies
To abuse someone's trust by leading them to act against their true interest
To corrupt someone's thoughts or feelings
To delude oneself about one's own wisdom or ability
G1818.detail:
1. To seduce means to deceive someone by diverting them from the truth through cunning. This is what the serpent did in Eden: he "seduced Eve by his cunning" (2 Corinthians 11:3), lying to her about the consequences of eating the forbidden fruit.
2. To abuse someone's trust means to lead them to do something that will harm or ruin them. False apostles "seduce the hearts of the simple" with flattering words that lead them away from the truth (Romans 16:18).
3. To corrupt means here to divert someone from their attachment to Christ. The Apostle fears that the thoughts of the Corinthians may be "corrupted" and turned "from the simplicity that is in Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:3).
4. To delude oneself: this is to willingly or carelessly deceive oneself. Paul exhorts: "Let no one deceive himself" by thinking himself wise according to this age (1 Corinthians 3:18).
G1818.origine: The Greek word ἐξαπατάω is formed from the prefix ἐξ- (which reinforces) and ἀπατάω (to deceive). This reinforced form emphasizes a complete, total deception that envelops or fully captures the victim. The base word ἀπατάω comes from a root that evokes the idea of diverting or leading away from the path. It is a voluntary and deliberate deception, often accompanied by seduction or flattery.
G1818.emploi: This verb appears six times in the New Testament, only in the Pauline epistles: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, 2 Thessalonians, and 1 Timothy. Paul uses it to describe different forms of spiritual deception. In Romans 7:11, sin "seduces" the believer by abusing the divine command. In Romans 16:18 and 2 Thessalonians 2:3, it is false teachers and seducers who use seduction. In 2 Corinthians 11:3, Paul refers to the precedent of the serpent seducing Eve. In 1 Timothy 2:14, it is the women who were "seduced" at the beginning. The verb can be used in the passive voice (to be seduced) to show the victim of the deception.
G1818.portee: This word warns the believer against a major spiritual reality: seduction. It comes from the enemy (the serpent in Eden), from false teachers, from sin itself, or from our own hearts. The Bible invites us to remain vigilant and to discern truth from cunning, to know ourselves honestly, and to remain attached to the simplicity of faith in Christ—far from flattering words that lead away from his person and his Gospel.

sens: At that very moment, without delay
Without preparation or warning
In an unexpected manner
G1819.detail:
1. "Immediately" expresses an action that occurs right away, at the present moment, without any interval between two events. In Mark 9:8, after the Transfiguration, as soon as the cloud withdrew, the disciples looked around — the word emphasizes that their reaction is instantaneous.
2. The word also carries the idea of suddenness and surprise: something happens unexpectedly, without notice. The disappearance of Moses and Elijah is sudden, and the disciples' vision instantly shifts from a heavenly scene to an ordinary reality.
3. In a biblical context, this suddenness often marks a divine intervention or a pivotal moment: it accentuates the extraordinary nature of what is happening and the impact on those who experience it.
G1819.origine: The Greek word ἐξάπινα (exapina) is an adverbial form derived from a root meaning "out" or "outside" (ex-) combined with a root evoking swiftness or sudden appearance. It belongs to a family of Greek words denoting suddenness: ἐξαπίνης and ἐξαίφνης are variants of the same word. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew פִּתְאוֹם (pithom), which literally means "suddenly."
G1819.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:8, during the Transfiguration of the Lord. Jesus was transformed, Moses and Elijah appeared to him, and a cloud enveloped them. When the cloud withdraws, "immediately" the disciples look around and see only Jesus. The adverb thus marks the abrupt transition from a supernatural vision to an ordinary reality, highlighting the suddenness of this transition and the astonishment of the disciples.
G1819.portee: This word reminds us that God sometimes acts unexpectedly and swiftly. For the disciple reading this passage, "immediately" invites vigilance: divine interventions can occur without warning, and they require a prompt response. The Transfiguration itself, with this suddenness, reinforces the reality of what happened and the importance of the moment for those who experienced it.

sens: To be in a total deadlock, unable to find a way out
To lose all hope, fearing that a situation is now beyond remedy
To be overwhelmed to the point of doubting one can survive
G1820.detail:
1. The word despair describes the state of one who is cornered, who sees absolutely no way out of their situation: it is an extreme perplexity, a feeling of being completely blocked. In 2 Corinthians 1:8, Paul says that the apostles "despaired even of life," meaning they were so overwhelmed by tribulation that they truly thought they would not survive.
2. It is also the absence of hope in the face of a calamity believed to be definitive: one sees no possibility for things to improve. The context of 2 Corinthians 1:8 shows suffering "beyond our strength," a weight so crushing that it crushes hope.
3. This notion is distinct from mere sadness: it is a state where trust is broken, where one even ceases to believe that they could be delivered. In 2 Corinthians 4:8, Paul defines himself in contrast as being in despair (the noun of the same verb), but "not driven to despair"—he shows that despair is a form of total abandonment.
G1820.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐξ (out of) and ἀπορέω (to be without resources, to be at a loss). The root ἀπορέω comes from ἀ (not) and πόρος (passage, way), hence the primitive image: not seeing a passage, being blocked. It is a word that literally paints a complete blockage, the impossibility of progressing or escaping.
G1820.emploi: Paul uses this verb twice in his correspondence with the Corinthians, in contexts of apostolic suffering. In 2 Corinthians 1:8, he describes the extreme distress suffered in Asia: the apostles are overwhelmed "beyond their strength" and come to "despair of life," which shows the real gravity of the persecution. In 2 Corinthians 4:8, the noun despair appears in a list of difficulties: the apostles are "hard pressed on every side, but not crushed," which reveals a victory of faith over circumstances. The word remains rare but powerful in expressing the limit of human endurance and the persistence of Christian trust despite everything.
G1820.portee: This word challenges the reader regarding the reality of Christian suffering: the apostles were not spared from affliction, but rather faced the abyss of despair. It also teaches that the hope of the Christian is not an escape from reality, but a strength that keeps us standing even at the gates of despair. Understanding this word helps recognize that apostolic perseverance is not stoic indifference, but a victory won over true fear.

sens: To send someone or something toward a goal, with intention and authority
To send someone away from oneself, to dismiss or remove them
To entrust a mission to someone by dispatching them somewhere
G1821.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to send someone or something to a destination. God sends his Son at the appointed time (Galatians 4:4), God sends his angel to deliver Peter (Acts 12:11). It is a voluntary, organized sending that comes from one who has authority.

2. To send away in the sense of making someone depart, often with a nuance of rejection or cessation. The rich are sent away empty (Luke 1:53), the servants are sent away after being mistreated (Luke 20:11). The word means: to push away, to dismiss, to separate from someone by putting them outside.

3. To send someone to accomplish a mission or to send them away while entrusting them to protection. Paul is sent to Tarsus (Acts 9:30), the brothers send Paul away to the sea to remove him from danger (Acts 17:14). It is a sending that protects or entrusts to a destination.
G1821.origine: The word is composed of three elements: *ex* (out of, outside), *apo* (away from, separation) and *stellō* (to send, to place, to set). This composition reinforces the idea of sending: one sends something or someone *out* of a place, *away* from a person. In Hebrew, the verb *šalaḥ* (to send) carries the same force: to send someone is to set them on a path with responsibility or a mission. The Greek verb faithfully captures this image of intentional and directional separation.
G1821.emploi: This verb appears 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and the epistles. Luke uses it to speak of the sending away of unfortunate servants (Luke 1:53; 20:10-11), while Acts often reserves it for salvific sendings: the angel sent to Peter, Paul sent on a mission, the message of the Gospel sent to the nations. In Galatians 4:4, it is the eschatological sending of the Son, a decisive moment in the history of salvation. The word can also be translated as "to depart" when the subject becomes the sent character who sets in motion. A constant nuance: *exapostellō* always marks a clear separation and a destination or a clear mission.
G1821.portee: This word reveals how God acts in history: he sends, he delegates, he entrusts missions. The sending of the Son in Galatians 4:4 is the heart of the Gospel, the act by which God intervenes to save. For the believer, understanding this verb shows that faith is not passive: God sends his messengers, his angels, his Spirit. It is also a call to recognize that we ourselves are sent, like Paul and the apostles, with a mission and protection.

sens: Arrive at the end of a period of time, to complete it
To provide someone with everything they lack to be complete and effective
To make something entirely finished and functional
G1822.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of time: when a period comes to an end, when one crosses the final limit. In Acts 21:5, the seven days of purification "are accomplished" — the designated period has ended. It is the simple idea of finishing a cycle.

2. Figuratively, "to accomplish" can also mean "to provide fully." In 2 Timothy 3:17, it is in the passive sense (passive voice): the man of God is "accomplished," meaning he possesses everything that makes him complete, prepared, equipped to accomplish "every good work." The word here denotes completion in the sense of perfection of equipment.
G1822.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "ἐξ" (to come out, extremity) and the root "ἄρτιος" which means "complete, perfect, having all its elements." Literally: "to make complete to the end." This root "ἄρτιος" appears in Romans 3:2 (useful) and evokes the idea of being adjusted, having all its parts. In biblical Hebrew, the verb חָבַר ("to unite, to join") in Exodus 28:7 conveys the same idea: assembling all the parts to form a functional whole.
G1822.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two distinct senses we have isolated. In Acts 21:5, it pertains to time: the seven days of stay in Tyre are "accomplished," meaning their natural term has been reached. In 2 Timothy 3:17, it describes spiritual equipment: the Scriptures "accomplish" the man of God by providing him with everything he needs. In both cases, the idea of fullness prevails: nothing is lacking, everything is in place.
G1822.portee: This word speaks to us of two important realities for the Christian. First, it reminds us that God's time has limits and stages (a trial, a wait "are accomplished"), which brings peace to the suffering. Secondly, in 2 Timothy 3:17, it affirms that Scripture alone is sufficient to make us "complete" to serve God — it is an encouragement to the sufficiency of God's word rather than dependence on human knowledge.

sens: To emit a bright and white light, like lightning or thunder
To be clothed in radiant and luminous splendor
G1823.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a sudden and dazzling brightness, that of lightning flashing from the sky. It is an intense, pure glow that illuminates with a sparkling white. Luke 9:29 uses it for Jesus' clothing during his transfiguration: "his clothing became dazzling white," a brightness so brilliant that it strikes the eyes with terror and admiration.
2. Figuratively, it means to become radiant, to wear a heavenly or divine splendor, as if a superhuman glory emanates from the body. The transfiguration is the perfect example: it is the divine shining through the human, a visible manifestation of the holiness and majesty of Christ.
G1823.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐξ ("out of," "toward the outside") and the verb ἀστράπτω ("to shine, to flash like lightning"). The root ἀστράπ- evokes lightning, thunder, the sudden brilliance of the sky. In Hebrew, Numbers 3:3 uses בָּרָק ("lightning") and Ezekiel 1:4 uses לָקַח in the sense of "to seize" to describe how divine light captures the gaze — it is the same idea of a splendor that emerges and imposes its presence.
G1823.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: Luke 9:29, at the moment when Jesus prays on the mountain and his disciples see his transfiguration. Its unique and majestic use emphasizes that it is an extraordinary event, out of the ordinary. The clothing becomes white "like lightning" — not by a change of fabric, but by a visible manifestation of the glory of Christ. It is a brightness that does not come from the outside, but bursts forth from within, from his revealed divine nature.
G1823.portee: This word reminds the reader that divine glory is luminous, radiant, irresistible. For the disciple, it is an invitation to desire spiritual transformation: to be filled with the Holy Spirit is to let this heavenly splendor shine through oneself. The dazzling whiteness of the transfigured Christ's clothing also foreshadows his final victory and glorious resurrection.

sens: Without delay, at the very moment
Immediately after an event
Without waiting, promptly
G1824.detail:
1. Without delay, at the very moment: the word denotes what happens at that very instant, without any time interval. When the king orders something, it is executed on the spot: in Acts 21:32, the tribune "at that moment" takes soldiers and runs toward the tumultuous crowd.
2. Immediately after an event: the word marks a rapid succession, an immediate consequence. In Acts 10:33, Peter reports that immediately after receiving the Lord's command, he hurried to send to Cornelius, and in Acts 11:11, the three messengers immediately presented themselves at the door.
3. Without waiting, promptly: the idea of eagerness and zeal. In Mark 6:25, Herodias' daughter hastens to immediately return to the king to present her request, fearing that he might change his mind.
G1824.origine: The word is composed of "ex" (to come out of, from) and "autes" (this same, this very hour). Literally, it means "from this very hour," that is, without delay, from the same instant. It is an expression from common Greek, very vivid and concrete: it evokes the idea of not leaving the present moment, of sticking to it, so to speak.
G1824.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and once each in Mark and Philippians. In Acts, it mostly describes orders obeyed without delay: the immediate sending of a person (Acts 10:33, 11:11, 23:30) or the rapid execution of a military command (Acts 21:32). In Mark 6:25, it emphasizes Herodias' daughter's eagerness to fulfill her request. In Philippians 2:23, it takes on a slightly different nuance: Timothy will be sent as soon as Paul sees "the outcome" of his situation, that is, at that moment, without further delay. In all cases, it is the immediacy that prevails.
G1824.portee: This word reminds us that in the New Testament, obedience to God and promptness go hand in hand. When God commands or when love calls to act, delay has no place. It is also a lesson in trust: do not delay, but rely on God's direction by moving forward without hesitation.

sens: To bring someone forth, to place them forward for a task or role
To bring someone back to life after death
G1825.detail:
1. To raise means to make appear, to bring forward, to establish someone to fulfill a purpose. It is the image of someone who is "lifted" or "raised" to play a role: God says to Pharaoh, "I have raised you up" (Romans 9:17), meaning he established him at that moment and in that place to manifest his power — Pharaoh is like lifted from nothingness to serve God's purposes.
2. To resurrect means to bring someone back to life, to make them live again after death. God "will also raise" the believers by his power (1 Corinthians 6:14), just as he raised the Lord Jesus: it is not just about "raising" them, but making them pass from death to eternal life.
G1825.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "egeirô" (to awaken, to raise) preceded by the prefix "ex" (out of, from). This intensive preposition reinforces the idea: it is not just about awakening, but about completely raising up, making arise. In Hebrew, this verb translates the word "ôur" (to awaken, to raise), used notably for God's action in raising his people or establishing a king.
G1825.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 9:17, it denotes the sovereign establishment of Pharaoh by God — not that God created him, but that he placed him at that moment to show his power. In 1 Corinthians 6:14, it denotes the resurrection of believers on the last day, parallel to the resurrection of Jesus. The context thus changes the meaning: providential establishment on one hand, resurrection on the other. Both uses emphasize God's sovereign action.
G1825.portee: This word reminds us that God does nothing passively: he raises men for his purposes, he intervenes in history. And above all, for the believer, he promises a certain resurrection, like that of Christ. It is a word of comfort and hope in the face of death.

sens: to leave a place, to depart
to leave quickly or at the right time
G1826.detail:
1. To go out, to leave a specific place: this is the simple movement of leaving a location. In Acts 13:42, when Paul and Barnabas "went out" of the synagogue, they were asked to return the following week. It is a departure without particular urgency, the natural conclusion of a meeting.
2. To leave or withdraw quickly, at the right moment: the word takes on a nuance of timing or efficiency. In Acts 20:7, Paul "was to depart the next day" — there is a plan, a scheduled time to leave. In Acts 27:43, the soldiers must "reach the land" by swimming — it is to escape danger and reach their goal. The underlying idea is that of an opportune or necessary action.
G1826.origine: The Greek word ἔξειμι is composed of ἐξ ("out of, outside") and εἶμι ("to go"). It is a simple movement verb but prefixed, which conveys the idea of crossing a threshold, of setting out towards the outside. The root ἐξ reinforces the idea of centrifugal direction — one does not move while staying in place; one goes outside, elsewhere.
G1826.emploi: This verb appears only four times in the New Testament, all in Acts. In Acts 13:42 and 17:15, it simply describes the end of a meeting or presence: Paul and Barnabas "go out" of the synagogue, Paul "departs" for Athens. In Acts 20:7, the context indicates a planned departure — Paul will leave tomorrow. In Acts 27:43, with the construction "ἐπί + accusative", the meaning shifts to "to head towards, to reach" — the swimmers "reach" the land to save themselves. The verb remains concrete in each occurrence: it is about physical movement, real displacement.
G1826.portee: This word reminds us that the life of the apostle — and that of the believer — is made up of departures, transitions, movements from one situation to another. Apostolic presence is never definitive in one place; it is a coming and going guided by the Spirit. This verb also invites us to notice the detail: a "departure" can be mundane (Acts 13:42) or salvific (Acts 27:43). It is the simple movement that punctuates the life of service.

sens: To pull, draw something or someone forcefully, towards oneself or elsewhere
To morally or spiritually lead towards evil, to seduce
G1828.detail:
1. The word paints the image of something being pulled or drawn with force — like pulling prey out of a trap. It is a physical movement of extraction or drawing.
2. In a figurative and moral sense, "to attract" refers to spiritual seduction: it is being drawn towards sin by one's own desires. James uses it this way: "each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desires" (James 1:14). Desire acts as a force that gradually pulls us towards evil, first by attracting us, then by ensnaring us.
G1828.origine: The word comes from the prefix "ἐξ-" (out of, outside) and the root "ἕλκ-" which means to pull or drag. This root evokes the concrete gesture of pulling something towards oneself or drawing it along. In the Greek Old Testament, this same verb translates the Hebrew "מָשַׁךְ" (to pull, to attract), notably in Genesis 37:28 where the brothers pull Joseph out of the pit.
G1828.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: James 1:14. In this key passage on temptation, James explains the mechanism of sin: desire attracts us like bait that draws the fish out of its safety. There is no passivity here: it is our own lust that pulls us towards evil. The word emphasizes the progressive dynamic of seduction — first the attraction, then the enticement (like prey), and finally the completed sin.
G1828.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize the reality of temptation: it is not an impersonal external force, but the fruit of our own desires that gradually draw us towards evil. Understanding this mechanism — that one is "drawn away" by one's lust — helps to discern and resist before being drawn too far. It is a call to spiritual vigilance.

sens: What an animal or a person expels from their stomach through the mouth
In a figurative sense, what one abandons or rejects
G1829.detail:
1. The word refers to the expulsion from the stomach: what is vomited, literally. In 2 Peter 2:22, it evokes the disgusting image of a dog returning to its vomit, as a way to illustrate the absurdity of returning to what has once been rejected.
2. In a figurative sense, it represents what one has abandoned or morally rejected. The image of vomiting suggests a physical and definitive break: one does not voluntarily return to what has been vomited. It is the idea of the proverb cited in 2 Peter: returning to one's vomit means going back to practices or beliefs that one had abandoned.
G1829.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb ἐξεράω (exerao), "to vomit" or "to reject", formed from the prefix ἐξ (ex), "out", and a root that expresses rejection. It is a rare and concrete word, very vivid: it depicts the physical act of rejection with starkness, which enhances its effectiveness in proverbs and moral warnings.
G1829.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:22. The apostle Peter cites a Hebrew proverb (Proverbs 26:11) to warn his readers against the danger of false teachers who, after having known the Gospel, fall back into their former sins. The image of the dog returning to its vomit illustrates the spiritual and moral folly of such a relapse: it is not only useless but repugnant.
G1829.portee: This word reminds the believer that they should never return to their former practices or beliefs, to what they have once rejected at the moment of their commitment to Christ. It also warns against seductive teachers who lead others into sin. The stark image of vomiting makes the message unforgettable: it is not an innocuous return, but a morally degrading fall.

sens: To search carefully, to investigate something thoroughly
To examine meticulously, to scrutinize
G1830.detail:
1. To research means to search for something with care and attention, going to the depths of things. The word evokes the image of an inquiry, an investigation where one does not settle for a first impression but digs, probes to understand. In 1 Peter 1:10, the prophets made "this salvation the object of their research": they did not just speak of the grace to come, they scrutinized it, they wondered how it would be realized.
2. To examine meticulously means to look carefully at all the details, as if reviewing them one by one. It is an active and focused form of attention, not a simple passive reflection.
G1830.origine: The Greek word comes from the prefix "ἐξ" (out, outside, intensity) added to "ἐρευνάω" (to search, to research). This prefix reinforces the idea of going beyond, of exploring completely. In the Greek Old Testament, the Hebrew verb "חָקַר" (haqar), which means to probe, to deepen, to scrutinize, was often translated by this word.
G1830.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Peter 1:10. Peter describes how the prophets of the Old Testament focused on the details of the salvation and grace that God promised. They did not speak by chance: they investigated, sought to understand what would happen, what their own prophecies meant. It is the image of pious men who want to grasp the full depth of what God reveals.
G1830.portee: This word reminds us that the prophets were not machines for prophesying: they were men who loved God and desired to understand His plans. This invites every reader to do the same: to research, to deepen their understanding of salvation rather than remain superficial. To research in Scripture is to honor the Word of God by giving it our serious attention.

sens: To move out of a place, to leave
To depart from one location to go elsewhere
To exit a closed or defined space
To emanate, to come from something or someone
To appear publicly, to become known
To be descended from, to come from (in a genealogical sense)
G1831.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to leave a place, a space. One goes out of a house, a prison, a region. Jesus goes out of the synagogue (Mark 1:29), the prisoner goes out of prison (Acts 16:36).

2. Sometimes the word emphasizes the movement toward a new place, not just the departure: "go" also translates the word when it carries this nuance (Matthew 24:26).

3. To leave a space also means to be separated from it, isolated: the apostle "leaves" a village without staying there (Luke 9:4).

4. In a figurative sense, the word describes what emanates, what flows: a rumor goes out from a city and spreads (Matthew 9:26), a voice comes out from heaven (Revelation 16:17).

5. To go out publicly means to appear, to become visible or known: demons go out of a possessed person (Mark 1:25), a word goes out to be made known.

6. To be descended from someone means to come from their lineage: the Messiah will come out of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:6), meaning he will be born there and originate from it.
G1831.origine: The word comes from the preposition "ex" (out of) and the verb "erchomai" (to go, to come). It literally means "to go out of." In Hebrew and Aramaic, it primarily translates the verb "yatsa" (to go out, to go outside), which evokes the movement of crossing a threshold, of escaping. This Hebrew verb also has figurative uses: a word goes out from the mouth, an order departs, one descends from a family. Greek has retained this richness of uses.
G1831.emploi: The verb is very frequent (213 occurrences) and plays a central role in the Gospel narratives and the Acts. The Gospels use it to describe the comings and goings of Jesus and the apostles: he goes out of the house, the synagogue, the tomb. In Matthew 2:6, it refers to the appearance of the Messiah in Bethlehem. Mark and Luke mainly use it for concrete movements, while John also uses it in a theological sense: Jesus has "come out" from God (John 16:27), meaning he comes from Him, that he is His envoy. In Acts, it often marks the departure of the apostles on mission. For demons, the word expresses their expulsion: they go out of a possessed person (Mark 1:25). Paul uses it in the sense of spiritual separation: those who go out from the assembly leave it for good (1 John 2:19).
G1831.portee: This simple verb reminds us that faith is not confined: it calls to go out, to testify, to reach out to others. Jesus himself continually goes out to meet the crowds and the sick. For the Christian, to go out also means to detach from sin (2 Corinthians 6:17) and to place oneself under the yoke of Christ. It is a word of action and movement that invites one not to remain passive in their spiritual life.

sens: To have the right to do something according to law or rule
To be authorized by an authority
To be lawful, in accordance with justice or morality
To be possible, feasible without hindrance
G1832.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is authorized by a law or established rule. The Pharisees reproach Jesus' disciples for doing what is not permitted on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:2): they violate the prohibition of work on that day. Similarly, only the priests are permitted to eat the showbread (Mark 2:26), as a temple law reserves it for them.
2. The word can also express permission given by someone who has authority. When Paul asks the tribune: "Is it permitted for me to say something to you?" (Acts 21:37), he is asking for the authorization of the one in command.
3. More broadly, it refers to what is just, lawful, or honest in the eyes of God. Paul writes: "Everything is permitted, but not everything is beneficial" (1 Corinthians 10:23), distinguishing what is technically allowed from what is truly profitable.
4. Finally, the word can simply mean that something is possible or feasible: something that is permitted is something that can be done without obstacle.
G1832.origine: The Greek ἔξεστι comes from the verb εἰμί ("to be") preceded by the prefix ἐξ ("out of"). The original image is that of what comes out, what is cleared, liberated: what is not held back or blocked. The impersonal form ("it is permitted") evokes a force or law that acts above us. It is a common word in classical Greek to express what is legal or authorized in the city.
G1832.emploi: The verb appears about thirty times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It is often used with an infinitive to express a prohibition or permission regarding an action. In the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, it regularly appears to discuss the debates between Jesus and the Pharisees about what is permitted to do on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:2, Mark 2:24, Luke 6:2) or about divorce (Matthew 19:3, Mark 10:2). In Acts and the Epistles, the word often carries a moral reflection: it is not enough to say that something is permitted for it to be beneficial or good (1 Corinthians 10:23, 1 Corinthians 6:12). Paul thus places the word in a tension between the freedom of the law and Christian prudence.
G1832.portee: This word helps the Christian distinguish legal permission from wisdom. For the believer, it is not enough to ask "do I have the right?"; one must also ask the question "is it really beneficial? Is it good for me and for others?" (1 Corinthians 10:23). Christian freedom goes beyond mere obedience to rules: it invites discernment of what truly builds faith and communal life.

sens: To conduct a thorough investigation, to seek to know the details of a matter
To ask questions to gather information
To interrogate someone to verify who they are
G1833.detail:
1. To examine carefully means to conduct a meticulous investigation to discover the truth. It is to seek to know precisely the details of a situation. Herod asks his magi to examine carefully the place where the child was born, meaning to go see precisely in Bethlehem and report the exact information to him (Matthew 2:8).

2. To inquire means to ask someone questions to learn something important. Jesus' disciples must inquire in every village to find a worthy man to welcome them (Matthew 10:11).

3. To interrogate someone means to ask them a question to verify or know their identity. The disciples do not dare to ask the resurrected Jesus, "Who are you?" because they know it is the Lord, but the verb suggests that one seeks to confirm or know who is before them (John 21:12).
G1833.origine: The Greek word ἐξετάζω (exetazō) is composed of the prefix ἐξ (ex, "out of") and the verb ἐτάζω (etazō, "to examine"). This composition emphasizes the idea of a thorough and methodical search. In ancient Hebrew, this verb often translates דָּרַשׁ (darash), which means "to seek, to inquire, to interrogate" or בָּחַן (bachan), "to test, to examine." The meaning is that of a voluntary and deliberate investigation to discover the truth.
G1833.emploi: The verb ἐξετάζω appears three times in the New Testament according to available sources: in Matthew (2:8 and 10:11) and in John (21:12). In Matthew, it describes Herod's inquiry about the birthplace of the Messiah and the instruction Jesus gives to his apostles to inquire before entering a house. In John, it characterizes the hesitant questioning of the disciples in the presence of the Resurrected One. In all these contexts, it involves a voluntary search for knowledge, conducted with care and intention.
G1833.portee: This word reminds us that seeking the truth is a serious and methodical act. For the believer, it evokes the importance of not accepting any information blindly: to examine, to verify, to inquire are responsible attitudes. But the example of the disciples in the presence of the Resurrected One also shows that sometimes, a certainty of the heart can surpass the need for questions.

sens: To expose, report what has happened
To describe the details of an event or action
To make known, reveal something to someone
To announce remarkable facts or wonders
G1834.detail: 1. The primary meaning of the word is to report, to tell the story of what has occurred. In Luke 24:35, the disciples "recount" what happened to them on the road to Emmaus; it is a simple report of lived events. 2. Often, this word describes a detailed and specific account: in Acts 21:19, Paul "recounts in detail" what God has done through his ministry. The idea is one of a structured presentation, not just a quick mention. 3. The word can also mean to make known, to reveal: in John 1:18, the Son has "made known" God; it is to make accessible what was hidden. 4. Finally, it serves to announce wonderful events: in Acts 15:12, they "recount" all the miracles and wonders that God has done; the word emphasizes the proclamation of admirable facts.
G1834.origine: The word comes from ἐξ ("out of") and ἡγέομαι ("to lead, show the way"). The basic image is that of showing the way, leading, which has extended to the figurative sense of "to unfold, expose in detail." In Hebrew, it often translates סָפַר (saphar), which means to recount, enumerate. The Greek word ἡγέομαι (without the prefix) also means "to lead, to consider."
G1834.emploi: The verb appears six times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts and the Gospel of John. In Acts (5 occurrences), it describes the oral recounting of events: the disciples recount their experiences with Jesus (24:35), Peter recounts how God chose the nations (15:14), Paul details his ministry (21:19). In all these cases, the context is that of a proclamation in an assembly, a narrative to bear witness. In John 1:18, the word takes on a deeper meaning: the Son "makes known" God, he reveals him. The word never denotes mere chatter, but always an intentional, structured account, often with spiritual or missionary significance.
G1834.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian testimony comes through recounting. Telling what God has done, what one has seen and experienced, is an essential form of mission and communion in the Church. It is also through the narrative that the Son reveals the Father to humanity. We are all called to "recount" the wonders that God accomplishes, not as rumors, but as thoughtful and sincere testimonies intended to edify and convert.

sens: The number 60
G1835.detail: 1. Sixty is a simple number in everyday language. In the parable of the sower, Jesus speaks of the grain that bears fruit "sixtyfold" (Matthew 13:8, 23), meaning that some grains produce sixty others. In geography, the distance between Jerusalem and the village of Emmaus is measured in "sixty stadia," an ancient unit of length (Luke 24:13). The minimum age required for a widow to be enrolled in the church's list of widows is "sixty years" (1 Timothy 5:9). In Revelation, sixty also appears in symbolic visions: the prophet sees fire coming down from heaven for "sixty" days, or a number related to the beast (Revelation 11:3, 12:6, 13:18). It is a simple number that measures, counts, or enumerates in biblical contexts.
G1835.origine: The Greek word ἑξήκοντα (hexēkonta) comes from the Indo-European root meaning "six" and "ten," formed by the composition: it denotes 6 × 10. Like all Greek numerical adjectives, it is invariant in form but can agree in gender with the noun it qualifies. The number sixty does not carry any particular theological weight in the Greek Bible; it is a common number for counting and measuring.
G1835.emploi: Sixty is a numerical adjective that appears 9 times in the New Testament. It is used in three main contexts. First, in the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:8, 13:23; Mark 4:8, 4:20), where it denotes the average yield of grain that falls on good soil, between the low yield (thirty) and the excellent yield (one hundred). Next, to measure a distance in stadia towards Emmaus (Luke 24:13). Finally, in Revelation (11:3, 12:6, 13:18), where it appears in the prophetic symbols of the last days. It is a common number, without variation in meaning according to the contexts.
G1835.portee: For the Christian reader, this number reminds us that Jesus takes seriously the diversity of spiritual fruit. In the parable, those who produce sixtyfold are not less approved than those who produce one hundred: there is a place for differentiated fruit according to each person's abilities. This reassures and encourages the believer who sees their growth as modest yet real.

sens: The day that immediately follows
The immediate sequence of an event
In the natural order of things
G1836.detail: 1. This word designates the day that comes right after another. In Luke 9:37, after the transfiguration on the mountain, "the next day, when they came down from the mountain, a great crowd met Jesus": it is simply the following day. 2. More broadly, it expresses the idea of immediate succession in time, "shortly after." In Acts 27:18, during the storm at sea, "the next day they threw the cargo overboard": events follow one after another. 3. The word can also carry the idea of natural continuity: things happen one after the other, as they should happen. In Acts 25:17, the judge "without delay, sat the next day on his tribunal": he acts without delay, in the normal course of things.
G1836.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "to have" (ἔχω) and evokes the idea of what "follows" or "comes after." It is a compound word that naturally expresses the succession and order of events in time.
G1836.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and the Gospel of Luke. It is used to mark a simple chronological transition: the passage from one day to another, or more broadly from one moment to another. In Luke 7:11 and 9:37, it introduces the events of the following day after significant moments (the visit of a centurion, the descent from the mountain of transfiguration). In Acts, especially in 21:1, 25:17, and 27:18, it marks the stages of a journey or a succession of judicial acts and maritime events. It is always a simple chronological notation, without particular nuance.
G1836.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible follows the real course of time, day after day. It also emphasizes that God acts in concrete history, day by day: after the transfiguration, after the storm, life continues and God remains at work. This invites us to recognize his presence not only in spectacular moments but also in the ordinary sequence of our days.

sens: To produce a sound that travels far
To be heard, to spread
To propagate, to diffuse widely
G1837.detail:
1. The verb retentir primarily describes the physical sound that resonates and extends: the word of the Lord "has resounded" (1 Thessalonians 1:8) like a trumpet or thunder that travels through the air. It is the image of a noise that emerges from its source and travels far.
2. Figuratively, retentir means "to be heard" and "to be known": the faith of the Thessalonians spread so widely that the apostle Paul did not need to speak of it — everyone had heard about it. The sound becomes a metaphor for fame and influence.
