3. The word suggests a powerful and irresistible diffusion: the word of the Lord does not remain confined to Thessalonica, but extends "through Macedonia and Achaia," then "everywhere." It is less a slow transmission than a natural and vigorous radiance.
G1837.origine: The Greek verb ἐξηχέω (exēcheō) is composed of the prefix ἐξ (ex-, "out of," "outside") and the root ηχ- (ēch-, which denotes sound, echo). It evokes the image of sound that bursts forth and disperses. The root ηχ appears in the word ἠχή (ēchē), "sound" or "echo," and the prefix ἐξ reinforces the idea of emergence, propagation. This verb translates the Hebrew הָמוֹן (hamon, "noise, tumult") in the Greek Old Testament: the sound that rises and flows everywhere.
G1837.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 1:8, in the passive voice ("has resounded"). Paul uses it to praise the burgeoning Church of Thessalonica: their conversion, faith, and faithfulness have become so visible and influential that it is spoken of everywhere in Macedonia and Achaia, without any need for a communication campaign. The word captures the vibrant, almost spontaneous effect of their testimony — like a sound that spreads naturally. It is a verb of impact and radiance.
G1837.portee: For the Christian, this verb reminds us that the living testimony of a Church, of an authentic life of faith, does not need publicity: it naturally resounds and spreads far beyond what one might expect. Visible faith produces a sound effect; it "is heard" in the world. It is an invitation to live faith in such a coherent and joyful manner that it inspires and influences those around us.

sens: Habitual practice, regular exercise of a faculty or skill
Experience gained through repetition
Habit that has become natural through training
G1838.detail:
1. Usage refers to the habitual and regular practice of an activity, one that is repeated until it becomes natural. In Hebrews 5:14, it is the exercise of moral judgment: those whose judgment is "trained by usage" have honed their discernment by applying it, just as one sharpens a blade by using it constantly.
2. This word also evokes concrete experience, what one has learned by doing. Usage is not theoretical knowledge, but the fruit of repeated practice until it becomes second nature.
3. By extension, usage is a firmly established habit: by using something repeatedly, one masters it and possesses it to the point that it belongs to them.
G1838.origine: The word ἕξις comes from the verb ἔχω (to have, to hold), which is the very root of Greek: to have something in one's possession or practice. Usage is what one "holds" through repeated practice, what one now possesses. The same root also gives rise to the word ἕξ-ις (stable state, acquired condition).
G1838.emploi: The word ἕξις appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 5:14. The author contrasts solid food with the milk of children: adults in faith are those who, through usage, have formed their moral discernment. It is a rare and precise word, chosen to express that spiritual maturity is forged through the patient and repeated exercise of judgment, not by teaching alone.
G1838.portee: This term teaches us that Christian maturity is not given outright: it is acquired by regularly exercising our moral discernment, applying the Word to life. It invites us not to remain passive in our walk of faith, but to actively cultivate our spiritual faculties through constant practice.

sens: To be struck with astonishment or amazement at something unexpected or wonderful
To lose one's senses, to be out of one's mind, to become like a fool
To be stunned to the point of being unable to react
G1839.detail:
1. To be astonished: it is the experience of someone who sees something that surpasses them, that surprises them deeply. When the crowd sees Jesus heal a mute demoniac in Matthew 12:23, they are "astonished" — seized with amazement at what they have just witnessed. In Acts 2:12, the apostles speak in various languages and the people are "in astonishment": it is the shock of the unexpected that paralyzes, that makes them stutter questions.
2. To lose one's senses: the word also designates someone who goes out of their right mind, who tilts towards madness. In Mark 3:21, Jesus' parents think that "he is out of his mind" — they believe he has lost his reason so astonishing and disturbing is his behavior. It is a tipping point: one moves from ordinary astonishment to mental panic.
3. To be stunned: when Simon the magician witnesses the miracles of the apostles (Acts 8:13), he is left astounded, unable to speak or move — it is astonishment that paralyzes, that suspends all normal reaction.
G1839.origine: The word comes from "ek" (out) and "histêmi" (to place, to stand): its initial image is that of someone being taken out of their place, being pulled from their normal position — they are "exported" out of themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words meaning primarily "to be confused" or "to be dismayed." This is why astonishment is never trivial in the Bible: it is always a moment when one is displaced from their equilibrium, when one steps outside of oneself.
G1839.emploi: The verb appears seventeen times in the four Gospels and Acts, never in the epistles. It primarily describes the reaction of crowds or disciples in response to the miracles of Jesus and the work of the Holy Spirit. Particularly in Mark (2:12, 5:42, 6:51), people are "astonished" at every miracle — it is a recurring theme. However, there is a nuance: in Mark 3:21, astonishment shifts to hostile misunderstanding (the parents think he is "out of his mind"), while in Acts 2:7 or 8:11, it is admiration in the face of a supernatural event. The word changes color depending on whether astonishment draws one closer to or further from faith.
G1839.portee: This word teaches us that encountering God and His work is never a neutral event: it shakes us, it pulls us out of our ordinary frame of understanding. The astonishment of the crowds and the apostles invites the reader to recognize in Jesus something that surpasses them — not just a circus wonder, but a manifestation of the divine. It is a call to leave behind our certainties and to allow ourselves to be moved by God.

sens: To have the strength or sufficient ability to accomplish something
To be capable of fully doing or understanding
G1840.detail:
1. The verb expresses the idea of having enough strength or power to perform an action. It refers to a complete ability, a sufficient aptitude. In Ephesians 3:18, Paul prays that Christians may have the strength to comprehend the spiritual dimensions of Christ's love — it is not merely about knowing, but having the deep capacity to grasp it.
2. The figurative sense extends to spiritual capacity: having the power, inner strength, or grace to accomplish something difficult or beyond our ordinary limits. It is the ability to do something beyond oneself.
G1840.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "ex" (out of, completely) and the verb "ischuo" (to have strength, to be strong). The preposition "ex" reinforces the idea: it is not only being strong, but having enough strength to go beyond, to transcend a limit. The root literally expresses physical strength, then extends to spiritual capacity.
G1840.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 3:18. Paul uses it to express his wish that believers receive from God the ability to grasp something wonderful: the dimensions of Christ's love. This is not ordinary power, but a spiritual aptitude given by the Holy Spirit, so that Christians can truly experience and understand the breadth of this love that surpasses all knowledge.
G1840.portee: This word reminds us that certain spiritual truths cannot be understood with our mere human intelligence: we need to receive from God the capacity to grasp them. The knowledge of Christ's love requires spiritual strength, a reinforcement by the Holy Spirit. It is an invitation to pray and rely on God's power to grow spiritually.

sens: the act of leaving, of quitting a place
death viewed as a departure from this world
G1841.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of going away, leaving one place for another. It is a movement, a change of location. In Hebrews 11:22, dying Joseph "mentions the departure of the sons of Israel," that is, their liberation and journey out of Egypt, the great event where God led His people to a new land.
2. Death is viewed as a departure: the one who dies leaves this world for an afterlife. In Luke 9:31, Moses and Elijah speak of the "departure" that Jesus "was about to accomplish at Jerusalem" — it refers to His death and resurrection. Similarly, in 2 Peter 1:15, Peter speaks of his "departure" as the moment he will die and leave this world.
G1841.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "ἔξ" (ek), which means "out of," and "ὁδός" (hodos), which means "way" or "road." Literally, it means "way out" or "exit." In Hebrew, it notably translates the word "matzá" (מוֹצָא), which has the same meaning of exit, departure.
G1841.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in a context of rupture or transition. In Luke 9:31, it refers to Jesus' departure from this world through His passion and resurrection — an event that Moses and Elijah, witnesses of the Transfiguration, celebrate as the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets. In Hebrews 11:22, it recalls the Exodus, the liberation of Israel from Egypt, which Joseph awaited by faith long before it occurred. In 2 Peter 1:15, it simply describes the apostle's impending death, his departure from this life.
G1841.portee: This word reminds us that the death of the Christian is not an absurd end, but a departure — a transition to the presence of God. Jesus Himself viewed His passion as an "exodus," a liberating new beginning, not only for Himself but for all redeemed humanity. For the believer, it invites us to see death not as annihilation but as a change of state, a passage.

sens: To completely destroy, annihilate without leaving any trace
To eliminate from a community, to cut off
To remove, to radically make disappear
G1842.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to totally destroy, to annihilate something or someone without leaving any trace. It is a destruction that goes all the way, leaving nothing standing. In Acts 3:23, Peter warns: anyone who does not listen to the prophet that God raises up will be "exterminated from among the people" — it is a complete disappearance, a radical removal from the community.
2. Closely related to the first sense, the word also expresses the idea of cutting someone off, eliminating them from within a community. It is not just about destroying, but about driving them away, permanently separating them from the people. It is a punishment aimed at ultimate banishment.
G1842.origine: The word is formed from two elements: "ex" (out of) and "olothreuō" (to destroy, to annihilate). The root expresses the idea of total destruction. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this Greek verb often translates the verb "karat" (to cut off), which in biblical language refers to the elimination of a person or lineage from the people of God. This notion of complete annihilation is characteristic of divine judgment in the Bible.
G1842.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 3:23, where Peter cites Deuteronomy 18:19 according to the ancient Greek version. Peter warns that anyone who refuses to listen to the prophet (Jesus) will be exterminated from among the people — this is the consequence of the voluntary and deliberate rejection of God's word. The context is that of divine judgment: it is a serious warning to those who refuse to submit.
G1842.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the seriousness of rejecting Christ and His word. It is not a passing threat or a temporary exclusion, but the total erasure of divine judgment. It is a warning: to listen to and obey the prophet that is Jesus is not optional; it is a matter of spiritual life or eternal death.

sens: To publicly acknowledge one's sins
To praise, to give glory to someone
To commit to doing something
G1843.detail:
1. To confess one's sins is to openly admit them before others or before God. John the Baptist invited those who came to be baptized to acknowledge their faults: "confessing their sins, they were baptized" (Matthew 3:6). Later, in the churches, believers "came to confess and declare what they had done" (Acts 19:18), thus unloading their shameful acts.
2. To praise someone or to give glory to their honor: this sense arises from the Greek verb that means to say the same thing as someone else. Jesus says to His Father: "I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth" (Matthew 11:25) — He agrees with the Father and acknowledges His greatness, His wisdom.
3. To commit to doing something: when Judas "committed" to the chief priests (Luke 22:6), he declared his agreement to help them, binding himself by his word.
G1843.origine: The Greek word combines a prefix (ἐξ, "out") with the verb ὁμολογέω (to say the same thing, to agree). The basic image is that of saying together, speaking with one voice. In Hebrew, this verb often translates the word יָדָה (yadah), which literally means "to lift the hand" — a gesture of acknowledgment and confession. This Hebrew root evokes the idea of publicly recognizing, giving thanks, submitting.
G1843.emploi: This verb appears 10 times in the New Testament. It predominates in the Gospels and in the early chapters of Acts, where the emphasis is on the confession of sins (Matthew 3:6, Mark 1:5, Acts 19:18). In Matthew and Luke, it also takes on the meaning of praise directed to the Father (Matthew 11:25, Luke 10:21), highlighting Jesus' agreement with the divine purpose. In Romans 14:11 and 15:9, the liturgical context reinforces this sense of public acknowledgment of God's greatness. James 5:16 encourages confessing "to one another." In Luke, it finally expresses Judas' commitment (Luke 22:6). Thus, the word encompasses both the admission of guilt and praise.
G1843.portee: Confessing one's sins is not a private humiliation: it is a courageous and public act of breaking with lies and shame. It opens the way to forgiveness and restoration. Praising the Father is also recognizing that God directs history and reveals His wisdom to the simple. It is an attitude of joyful submission to His will.

sens: To compel someone to take a solemn oath, under the authority of God's name
To demand a response by invoking a sacred authority
G1844.detail:
1. To adjure someone is to compel them to take an oath, or to swear to tell the truth, by reminding them of God's authority. It is a serious and solemn formula. When the high priest adjures Jesus by saying, "I adjure you by the living God" (Matthew 26:63), he places Jesus under the obligation to respond in the name of God himself — as if God were the guarantor of this question.
2. The word evokes the idea of a summons: the one who adjures commands the other to speak the truth or to act, invoking a higher, divine power that makes silence or lying impossible.
G1844.origine: The Greek word comes from ἐξ ("out of, completely") and ὁρκίζω ("to make swear, to compel to an oath"), which is derived from ὅρκος ("oath"). In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses אָלָה ("curse, imprecation") or שָׁבַע ("to swear, to take an oath") to express the same idea. The word suggests the imposition of a solemn obligation before God.
G1844.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament according to the Segond: in Matthew 26:63, during the interrogation of Jesus before the Sanhedrin. The high priest uses this formula to force Jesus to answer the most serious question — that of his identity as Messiah. It is an act of religious authority, where the chief priest invokes the living God to make the question irresistible. The context shows that "to adjure" is a last resort to obtain an explicit declaration from the accused's mouth.
G1844.portee: This passage shows the difference between human questioning and divine obligation. The high priest hopes that Jesus, placed under the power of the oath in God's name, will be compelled to respond. However, Jesus answers freely and in the way he chooses. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that no one can be compelled to speak by religion or intimidation: only the grace of God opens the heart.

sens: one who expels evil spirits by words of power
one who pronounces formulas or invocations to cast out demons
itinerant who practices this profession
G1845.detail:
1. An exorcist is someone who drives out evil spirits from a person's body by pronouncing words or formulas believed to have power over these spirits. The word comes from the idea of "expelling" (ex-) and "conjuring" (orki-), meaning to force something out through a binding word.
2. More broadly, it refers to one who "conjures" — that is, who speaks with authority, pronouncing a formula intended to compel obedience, especially from evil spirits. This was a common practice in the Jewish and pagan world of the first century.
3. In Acts 19:13, we encounter itinerant Jewish exorcists, meaning they traveled from city to city to offer their services in casting out demons. These men had a profession: they made a living by expelling spirits.
G1845.origine: The Greek word ἐξορκιστής comes from ἐξορκίζω ("to expel by conjuration"), composed of ἐξ ("out of") and ὅρκος ("oath, word of authority"). It expresses the idea of forcing something — here an evil spirit — to obey through a word endowed with power. This practice is attested in ancient Judaism: exorcists are found in rabbinic literature and in apocryphal texts, who used names, formulas, or special techniques to expel demons.
G1845.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:13. In this passage, Paul is ministering in Ephesus, a major center of idolatry and magical practices. Local Jewish exorcists — whom Luke describes as "itinerant," showing that they moved from city to city to practice their trade — attempt to exploit the name of Jesus as a magical formula to cast out demons. They try to invoke Jesus over the possessed by saying, "I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches!" Their attempt fails dramatically: the demon reacts violently and overpowers them. This episode illustrates the contrast between human techniques and the supernatural power of God in Christ.
G1845.portee: This passage teaches that the name of Jesus is not a magical formula that can be manipulated at will, nor can it be simply pronounced with the right words. It is the power of God himself, who only submits to one who has a living relationship with Christ. Authentic deliverance does not come from religious techniques or correctly spoken words without faith, but from the very person of Jesus and his absolute authority over evil spirits.

sens: To remove by digging or forcing
To take away by violent effort
To take away in a figurative sense, to deprive oneself
G1846.detail: 1. The literal meaning is to remove something by digging or forcing: in Mark 2:4, they tear off the roof to lower the paralytic — it requires really breaking through, digging into the structure. 2. The meaning extends to any violent and difficult removal: the image is one of energetic tearing away. 3. Figuratively, in Galatians 4:15, Paul tells the Galatians that they would have wanted to tear out their eyes — that is, to deprive themselves of something very dear, out of love for him. The word retains the idea of intense effort and forced separation.
G1846.origine: The word is composed of the preposition « ek » ("out of") and the verb « orussô » ("to dig, to bore"). The starting image is that of digging, the work of turning over the earth. The prefix « ek » reinforces the idea: digging to bring out, to remove completely. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew « naqar » ("to dig, to pierce").
G1846.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Mark 2:4, the men carrying the paralytic literally put it in the sense of the word: they tear off the roof of the house to lower him down to Jesus — it is a spectacular physical act. In Galatians 4:15, Paul uses it hyperbolically and affectionately: he speaks of tearing out his eyes to give them to someone — it is the extreme expression of love and devotion, the idea that one would deprive oneself of what is most precious. The word moves from the concrete to the figurative, but always retains the idea of a costly effort.
G1846.portee: This word shows us living faith in action: in Mark 2:4, the men do not hesitate to do anything to bring their friend to Jesus — they break the roof! It is the image of persistent intercession and devotion. In Galatians 4:15, Paul reminds Christians that authentic brotherly love compels one to deprive oneself of what one cherishes most. For us today, it is an invitation to examine the true strength of our faith and Christian friendship.

sens: to treat someone with disdain, to regard them as worthless
to reject with contempt
to reduce to nothing in esteem
G1847.detail:
1. To despise means to treat someone or something with a profound lack of esteem, as if it has no value. It is to look down on it, to consider it negligible. In Mark 9:12, Jesus announces that he "must suffer many things and be despised": people will treat him as if he is worth nothing, without respect or consideration.
2. This contempt is often accompanied by rejection: the despised person is pushed away, refused recognition or honor. It is a hostile judgment that excludes someone from community or honor.
3. The word also evokes the idea of reducing to nothing: contempt nullifies someone's dignity, rendering it invisible in the eyes of others.
G1847.origine: The Greek word is composed of "ex" (out of) and "ouden" or "outhen" (nothing). The basic image is that of "coming out of nothing" or "treating as nothing." It is the same root found in "exoutheneō," a more common variant. The word translates several Hebrew terms expressing contempt or rejection: "buz" (to despise), "bazah" (to humiliate), "maas" (to reject), or "bus" (to trample underfoot).
G1847.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:12, in the prediction of the Passion. Jesus states that the Son of Man "must suffer many things and be despised." This context shows that the contempt in question is not a mere insult, but a deep hostility and rejection that accompany suffering. It is part of the humiliation that Jesus would endure. The verb emphasizes the seriousness of this contempt: it is not a slight disdain, but a denial of the dignity and worth of the person.
G1847.portee: This word invites the reader to measure the depth of Jesus' humiliation. To despise is not only to do harm; it is to deny the very worth of someone. By announcing that he would be despised, Jesus willingly accepts this extreme humiliation — not only physical suffering but rejection, invisibility in the eyes of men. For the Christian, it is a call to consider this cost of redemption and to never belittle one whom God honors.

sens: to treat someone or something with contempt, to consider it worthless
to disregard, to take little account of
to reject, to push away
to humiliate, to treat with disdain
G1848.detail:
1. To despise means to consider someone or something as unworthy of respect or worthless. It is a harsh judgment of the heart that manifests as displayed contempt. In Romans 14:3, we see this pitfall: strong Christians must not despise the one who has dietary scruples, for it is God who has welcomed him.
2. The word can also mean to take no account of something, to ignore or disdain it. In Luke 18:9, the self-righteous Pharisees made little account of others — they treated them as negligible.
3. To reject is a related meaning: it is to refuse someone or something after judging it unworthy. In Acts 4:11, the stone that you builders rejected has become the cornerstone — it did not seem worthy to be kept.
4. To humiliate and to treat with disdain go together: to despise is also to publicly belittle. In Luke 23:11, Herod treated Jesus with contempt: he dressed him in a splendid robe to mock him, humiliating him before his guards.
G1848.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: ἐξ- ("out of," "completely") and -ουθενέω (formed from οὐθείς, "no one, nothing"). The basic image is therefore that of a thing or person treated as nothing, completely rejected. It is an intensive verb: it is not a mere indifference, but an active and contemptuous rejection.
G1848.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Gospels. It often designates the danger of despising those whom God has welcomed: in Romans 14:3 and 14:10, Paul warns Christians not to despise one another over matters of conscience. In 1 Corinthians 1:28, the word describes God's strategy: God chooses the despised things of the world to nullify the powerful. In Acts 4:11, it is the stone from Psalm 118 that has been rejected. In Luke 23:11, it is the very humiliation of Jesus by Herod. The meaning nuances: sometimes it is a proud judgment among believers (Romans), sometimes a collective refusal (Acts, Luke), sometimes a divine choice of what is worthless in the eyes of the world (1 Corinthians).
G1848.portee: This word calls the believer to vigilance against the pride of their own judgment. To despise a brother whom God has welcomed is to contradict God himself. But it also encourages: the despised in the eyes of the world — the weak, the rejected — is precisely the one whom God elevates and honors. Jesus himself was despised and rejected, and it is through this humiliation that he became the cornerstone.

sens: Freedom and power to act according to one's own will
Legal right to exercise a command or function
Power of one who governs or judges
Scope of authority of a leader or authority
Supernatural or cosmic power
G1849.detail:
1. Authority is primarily the freedom and power to do something, to put into action what one is capable of doing. This is why Jesus says: "I have come in Galilee" and "no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down voluntarily" (John 10:18), affirming his own power to decide.
2. Authority is the legitimate right to exercise a function, to command or order. Jesus teaches "as one having authority, and not as their scribes" (Matthew 7:29): he does not cite masters, he speaks with the sovereign right of one who knows the truth.
3. Authority is the judicial and executive power: the one who can render justice, punish or grant mercy. Pilate says to Jesus: "Do you not know that I have the power to release you, and the power to crucify you?" (John 19:10).
4. Authority can also refer to the territory or domain over which this power is exercised. Herod was interested in Jesus "because of the great things being told about him" and wanted to know what authority he spoke with (Luke 23:7).
5. Authority extends to the supernatural powers that reign in the invisible universe. Paul speaks of "authorities" and "powers" in the heavenly places (Ephesians 1:21), the spiritual beings that dominate the invisible worlds.
G1849.origine: The word comes from the root ἔξεστι (« it is permitted »), formed from « ex » (out of): it first designates what is permitted, hence the freedom to act. In ancient Greek, this word gradually grows in meaning: from simple permission, it moves to the right to exercise a charge, then to the power itself and to the one who holds it. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew « שָׁלְטָן » (shâltan), which also means "dominion" or "empire." This family of words is very close to δύναμις (power): where δύναμις emphasizes the brute force capable of acting, ἐξουσία emphasizes the right and legitimacy of that force.
G1849.emploi: This word is used 93 times in the New Testament, especially by Luke and Paul, and spans all contexts of human and divine existence. In a narrow sense, it describes Jesus' authority to teach (Mark 1:22), his power to forgive (Mark 2:10), that of his apostles (Matthew 10:1). In a broader sense, it designates civil and judicial power: that of Pilate (John 19:11), of Roman magistrates (Luke 12:11), of governors (Luke 20:20). Even more broadly, Paul uses this word to speak of the right the apostle has to be supported by the Church (1 Corinthians 9:4-6) or the authority he claims to build up his communities (2 Corinthians 13:10). Finally, the word reaches its highest significance when it evokes spiritual powers: angels (Colossians 1:16), demons (Ephesians 2:2), and even "all authority" in heaven that the Father has given to the Son (Matthew 28:18).
G1849.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize where true authority comes from: it is not simply brute force, but the right that comes from God. Jesus teaches with authority because he is the Son of the Father and knows the truth; those who follow him receive the right to become children of God (John 1:12). For everyone, the word reminds us that there are legitimate authorities—civil, ecclesiastical—that are worthy of respect, but also that none surpasses that of God. It also helps to understand the invisible battles: the Christian does not wrestle only against flesh and blood, but against the "authorities" of evil (Ephesians 6:12), and the Church is called to manifest the wisdom of God in the face of these powers.

sens: Exert power, command
Dominate someone, have power over them
Subjugate, keep under domination
Have the right of disposal over something
G1850.detail:
1. To exercise authority: this is what kings do when they govern their nations. In Luke 22:25, Jesus speaks of kings who "dominate" the nations, that is, who exercise their royal power over them.
2. To dominate a person: to have power over someone, to control them. This is the idea of master over slave or leader over subordinate.
3. To subjugate or keep under domination: to reduce someone to forced obedience. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6:12 that he will not allow anything to "enslave" him, meaning he will refuse to fall under the domination of anything.
4. To have the right of disposal: to possess authority over something, to have the right to use it. In 1 Corinthians 7:4, Paul teaches that the wife does not have "authority" over her own body, but the husband does—he can dispose of it, and vice versa.
G1850.origine: The word comes from ἐξουσία (exousia), which means "authority" or "power." This word primarily designates the legal right or legitimate power to do something, hence the idea of power as right. In Greek, the verb formed from this noun expresses the action of putting this right into practice. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word שָׁלַט (shalaṭ), which means "to reign" or "to dominate."
G1850.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament. In Luke 22:25, it describes how the kings of the nations exercise their authority in governing. In 1 Corinthians 6:12, Paul uses it in the passive voice to say that no habit or passion should "dominate" or "enslave" him. In 1 Corinthians 7:4, it designates the right that husband and wife each have over the other's body in marriage: each has "authority" over their spouse's body. The word thus oscillates between the idea of political power (Luke), restrictive control (1 Corinthians 6), and marital right (1 Corinthians 7).
G1850.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on authority: the authority they have, the authority to which they submit, and the authority that should not dominate them. Paul particularly warns that even what is permitted should not "enslave" us—we must remain free in Christ and not let ourselves be controlled by our appetites or habits. For couples, it reminds us that respecting the other’s body means recognizing that one does not have sole "authority" over it, but that there is a sharing. It is a call to the wise and mutual exercise of the power we receive.

sens: That which stands out, rises above the rest
Distinction, superiority of rank or status
Persons who occupy the highest places
G1851.detail:
1. The word primarily designates something that stands out, that projects: thus a rock outcropping. This is the literal sense, an image of something that "exceeds."
2. In a figurative sense, it describes a superiority, an excellence that places someone above others. It is a natural or recognized distinction.
3. It is used to designate the eminent persons themselves—those who enjoy this distinction. In Acts 25:23, Paul is presented before "the prominent ones" (literally: "those who had preeminence") of the city, that is, the notables, the dignitaries who occupied the highest places in the city.
G1851.origine: The word comes from the verb « exéchô » (to stand out, to project). It is formed from the root « ex » (out of): the basic idea is thus a projection, something that exceeds or surpasses. The Hebrew « shèn » (Job 39:28) designates a tooth or a ridge—something that stands out—and the Greek word has taken it up to express everything that "is out of the ordinary."
G1851.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 25:23. Paul, a prisoner, is brought before Governor Festus to be heard; for this solemn occasion, King Agrippa and Queen Berenice present themselves "in great pomp," accompanied by the tribunes and the "prominent ones" of the city—that is, the civil authorities, the magistrates who enjoyed a superior status and public recognition.
G1851.portee: This word invites the believer to note that even a prisoner, a man seemingly without power or rank, stands before the highest dignitaries. It is an image of how God can place his own face to face with the powerful to bear witness. It also reminds us that true preeminence—the lasting value—is not what the world recognizes, but what God confers.

sens: to bring someone out of sleep
to end someone's inaction or indifference
G1852.detail:
1. To wake someone who is sleeping: this is the literal and concrete meaning of the word. The verb describes the action of pulling a person from sleep. Jesus uses it when speaking of Lazarus: "Lazarus, our friend, is sleeping; but I am going to wake him up" (John 11:11). The word emphasizes this transition from sleep to wakefulness.
2. Figuratively, to wake up can also mean to bring someone out of inaction, indifference, or forgetfulness. Sleep becomes the image of a kind of moral or spiritual torpor from which someone is awakened.
G1852.origine: The Greek word is composed of "ek" (out of, outside) and the verb "hypnizō" (to put to sleep, to slumber), which themselves come from "hypnos" (sleep). The basic idea is therefore: "to come out of sleep." The Old Testament uses related Hebrew verbs like "yaqetz" (to awaken, to wake up) to express this same notion of transition from sleep to wakefulness.
G1852.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:11, where Jesus speaks of Lazarus's death using a veiled expression: he says that Lazarus "is sleeping" and that he will "wake him up." The disciples, not initially understanding that Jesus is speaking of death, interpret his words in the literal sense of ordinary sleep. This unique occurrence shows how Jesus uses the language of sleep to evoke death while affirming his power of resurrection. The word thus highlights the contrast between the appearance of rest and the reality of death that only the Lord can conquer.
G1852.portee: This word from Jesus teaches the reader that death, for the believer, is not a definitive end but a "sleep" from which the Lord alone can awaken us. It affirms his power over death and nurtures the hope of resurrection. It also reminds us of the importance of listening to the words of Christ attentively, as they often contain a depth hidden beneath simple language.

sens: Brought out of sleep, awakened
Suddenly emerged from a state of unconsciousness or torpor
G1853.detail:
1. The word describes the state of someone who has just woken up, who has left sleep. In the literal sense, it means moving from sleep to wakefulness. In Acts 16:27, the jailer in Philippi "awoke" suddenly when an earthquake shook the prison: he moved from a deep night sleep to full alertness.
2. More broadly, the word can describe a sudden awakening from torpor, unconsciousness, or moral and spiritual drowsiness. The image remains that of moving from darkness and inertia to consciousness and action.
G1853.origine: The word is composed of "ἔξ" (out of, outside) and "ὕπνος" (sleep). The etymological image is simple: to come out of sleep. This composition emphasizes the sudden and complete nature of the transition from the state of sleep to the state of wakefulness. The Greek word conveys a concrete and immediate reality well known to all.
G1853.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:27. This is at the moment when an earthquake opens the doors of the prison where Paul and Silas are imprisoned in Philippi: the jailer, abruptly awakened from sleep, realizes the disaster and prepares to commit suicide, believing that the prisoners have escaped. The context emphasizes the sudden and dramatic nature of the awakening.
G1853.portee: This passage shows us how an unexpected circumstance (the earthquake) can awaken someone to a new reality. For the Christian reader, it also evokes the spiritual idea of awakening of the conscience: it is often through providential events that God awakens sleeping hearts and leads them to turn to him. The jailer, physically awakened, will soon be spiritually awakened and embrace the faith.

sens: external space to a place
action of going out of a space
people who are not in the Christian community
person or thing rejected, excluded
G1854.detail:
1. **Outside** primarily designates external space: what is outside a house, a city, a closed place. When it is said, "your mother and your brothers are outside" (Mark 3:32), it refers to people waiting outside. The salt thrown "outside" (Matthew 5:13) is expelled from the house, having become useless.

2. The word is used to express the action of going out, of going outside. When Peter "went outside" and wept (Matthew 26:75), he left the place where he was. It conveys the idea of movement outward, of breaking away from a space.

3. **Outside** takes on a crucial figurative meaning: it designates those who are "outside" the Church, the unbelievers or those excluded from the community. Paul writes: "Do you not judge those who are outside?" (1 Corinthians 5:12), contrasting the faithful with non-believers. It is a spiritual status, not a geographical location.

4. The word can also mean to be rejected or excluded: the authorities "threw outside" the healed blind man (John 9:34) because he confessed Jesus. To be outside is to be separated, set apart.
G1854.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition **ἐξ** ("out of") and functions as an adverb or preposition. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it translates **חוּץ** ("outside", "outdoors"), which has the same concrete and figurative scope. The root suggests the idea of crossing a boundary, moving from inside to outside. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word regularly translates passages where it speaks of coming out of Egypt or crossing a border.
G1854.emploi: The word appears 64 times in the New Testament. It is first used in the concrete spatial sense: Jesus's mother and brothers "outside" (Mark 3:32, Luke 8:20), the disciples sent outside (Matthew 10:14), Peter who goes out to weep (Matthew 26:75). Gradually, it takes on a figurative and communal sense: Paul opposes "those outside" (non-believers) to the faithful of the Church (1 Corinthians 5:12-13). It also designates those who are expelled or rejected: the blind man "cast outside" because he believes in Jesus (John 9:34), or the salt thrown outside because it has lost its flavor (Matthew 5:13). This shift from spatial to communal and moral is characteristic of its biblical usage.
G1854.portee: This word invites reflection on our spiritual boundaries. Jesus says that it is from the heart that evil thoughts come (Matthew 15:19): being "outside" is not an external limit to fear, but a reality that comes from within us. Being "outside" reminds believers of their position of grace: the Church must judge those who are members, not the unbelievers (1 Corinthians 5:12). Finally, the salt thrown outside or the body delivered outside (Hebrews 13:11-13) evokes sacrifice: Jesus accepted to go outside the city to be crucified, revealing to us that God meets his faithful well beyond any human limit.

sens: The space or the outside of a thing
What is visible, apparent, in contrast with the hidden interior
The outer part of the body or physical appearance
People outside a group or community
G1855.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning refers to the material outside, what is out there: Jesus says, "nothing from outside that enters a man can defile him" (Mark 7:18), speaking of what comes from outside the body.
2. Often, the word expresses the contrast between the outer appearance and the inner reality: the Pharisees clean "the outside of the cup" but the inside remains "full of extortion" (Matthew 23:25), and "outwardly" they appear righteous, but "inwardly" they are full of hypocrisy (Matthew 23:28).
3. Applied to physical appearance: the ornament "of the outside" should not be what predominates among women (1 Peter 3:3), meaning the adornments and outer clothing.
4. Used to refer to people from the outside, foreign to a community: a bishop must have "a good testimony from those outside" (1 Timothy 3:7), meaning non-Christians or people from the pagan world.
G1855.origine: The word comes from the root ἔξω ("out"), with the suffix -θεν indicating origin or source ("from where"). It is an adverb formed naturally to answer the question "where does this come from?" — hence the primary meaning "from outside" or "from the outside." The perpetual contrast in the New Testament between ἔξωθεν (outside) and ἔσωθεν (inside) reflects the biblical concern for the inner reality of the soul in relation to outer appearances.
G1855.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, and in the epistles. In the Synoptics, it systematically opposes the outside to the inside: in Jesus' teaching on ritual purity (Mark 7 and parallels), and then in his criticisms of the Pharisees who care for their outer image (Matthew 23). In the epistles, the meaning broadens: it sometimes refers to physical appearance (1 Peter 3:3), sometimes to those who are outside the Christian community (1 Timothy 3:7), and sometimes to a geographical area (Revelation 11:2, the outer court of the temple). The nuance is always the same: what is visible, accessible, or on the edge, in contrast to what is hidden, essential, or inner.
G1855.portee: This word invites the reader to look beyond appearances. The Bible uses "outside" to disturb those who judge by appearances: our outer actions matter only if they reflect a transformed heart. For the Christian, it is a call to authenticity and purity of heart before any outward demonstration of piety.

sens: To drive someone or something out of a place, to forcefully push them away
To push a boat toward the shore
G1856.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to chase or expel: to firmly and definitively remove someone from a place. In Acts 7:45, God "chases" the nations before the Israelites: this is not a simple request to leave, but a powerful action that removes the inhabitants of the promised land to make way for Israel.
2. The second, more specialized meaning appears in Acts 27:39: it refers to pushing a ship toward the shore. The shipwrecked sailors attempt to steer their boat toward the shore to run it aground safely — a physical and concrete action that utilizes the movement of "pushing" of the word.
G1856.origine: The word combines the prefix "ex-" (outward, outside) and the verb "ôthéo" (to push, to drive away). This root "ôthéo" evokes the fundamental image of giving an impulse, to chase by force. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates a Hebrew verb meaning "to push away" or "to expel." The prefix "ex-" intensifies the idea of movement outward: it is not just about moving, but about going out, leaving definitively.
G1856.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 7:45, it is God who acts as the subject: he chases the idolatrous peoples from the promised land to give it to Israel — a divine act of expulsion related to the conquest of the land. In Acts 27:39, it is the crew of a ship in peril trying to push the boat toward the shore, seeking safety through this maneuver. Both uses retain the idea of forced movement: to chase from a place, or to direct forcefully toward a goal.
G1856.portee: Seeing God "chase" the nations before Israel reminds the reader that the possession of the promised land was not due to the military strength of the Israelites, but to divine action. For the Christian, it is a sign that God acts powerfully for his promises. In the story of the shipwreck, seeing the sailors "push" the ship toward safety shows how, in the face of peril, man and God cooperate: men act according to their ability, and God preserves his servant Paul alive.

sens: What is outside, beyond the limits
The darkness, the gloom of the outside
The definitive separation from God and his light
G1857.detail:
1. The word first designates what is located outside, beyond the borders or walls: it is the opposite of the inside. It is the basic physical image: to be outside is to be far from the inside.
2. In the three passages of Matthew, this word qualifies the "outer darkness": a blackness that reigns outside, far from any light. Jesus uses it three times (Matthew 8:12, 22:13, 25:30) to describe the place where those who do not live according to God's will are cast.
3. The "outside" thus becomes an image of the eternal separation from God, who is light. Those who are cast into the outer darkness weep and gnash their teeth: it is the expression of their despair.
G1857.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "out of," "outside" (ἔξω). It is a comparative adjective that emphasizes what is located beyond, further out. In Hebrew, it often translates the word "chiçon" (חִיצוֹן) which has the same meaning: what belongs to the outside, to the exterior.
G1857.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the Gospel of Matthew, and in the very words of Jesus. Each time, Jesus associates it with the "outer darkness" to describe the fate of those who are not his true disciples or who have failed to fulfill the Father's will. The context varies slightly: first the children of the kingdom who do not believe (Matthew 8:12), then a guest without a wedding garment (Matthew 22:13), and finally the servant who hid his talent (Matthew 25:30). But the image remains identical: rejection, exclusion, weeping, and gnashing of teeth.
G1857.portee: This word challenges each reader regarding their belonging to the Kingdom. Being "inside" or "outside" is not a simple geography: it is a matter of relationship with Jesus and trust in his word. The image of the "outer darkness" expresses not an arbitrary penalty, but the reality of the choice made during earthly life: those who reject the light find themselves in darkness, separated from God. It is a call not to neglect the call of the Kingdom.

sens: Fulfill the rites and festivities of a religious feast
Solemnly observe an event by commemorating it
Live in the joy and gladness of a celebration
Rejoice spiritually in communion with others
G1858.detail: 1. Celebrating a feast means fulfilling the rites, meals, and festivities prescribed to honor a deity or commemorate an event — just as the Jews observed Passover, the Feast of Tabernacles, or Pentecost under the Law. 2. In the figurative sense that Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 5:8, it means to solemnly observe and commemorate a significant event by imitating its sacred character: "Let us celebrate the feast" becomes an image for living up to the sacrifice of Christ, as one would during a true feast. 3. This implies an atmosphere of joy, purity, and moral integrity — one does not celebrate Passover "with old leaven, with the leaven of malice and wickedness," but "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." 4. For the Christian, it is to live in an attitude of joy, gladness, and communion, as if every day were a feast in honor of Jesus Christ.
G1858.origine: The verb comes from the noun ἑορτή (heortē), "feast" — that is, a solemn assembly, a day of rejoicing established by religious law. In Hebrew, the word חָגַג (hagag) carries the same idea: to fulfill a festive pilgrimage, to rejoice before the Lord during prescribed feasts. The image is that of a joyful and orderly gathering.
G1858.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 5:8. Paul uses it allegorically: after instructing the Corinthians to expel the fornicator (1 Co 5:1-5), he exhorts them to "celebrate the feast" of Christ, the Passover sacrifice, by ensuring their own moral purity. The verb transposes to Christian life the idea of the great Jewish feast of Passover, transforming the entire existence of the believer into a perpetual celebration of the redemption brought by Jesus.
G1858.portee: This word reminds the Christian that faith in Christ is not a morose or austere attitude, but a deep and orderly joy. Celebrating the feast of Christ means living with gladness, casting out the leaven of malice and putting on moral purity — a visible sign that one truly tastes the grace of redemption. It also acknowledges that Christ is our sacrificed Passover, and that we pass from spiritual death to new life.

sens: Religious and festive celebration held on a fixed date in the Jewish calendar
Gathering of crowds on the occasion of such a celebration
Period or moment of the celebration
Opportunity to fulfill a duty or religious practice
G1859.detail:
1. A feast is a major religious celebration in the Jewish calendar, set on a regular date and marking an important event or period in the history and faith of Israel. Jesus and his parents "went every year to Jerusalem for the Feast of Passover" (Luke 2:41), which shows that these feasts structured the life of the people in a recurring and expected manner. The main feasts mentioned are Passover, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and the Feast of Tabernacles.
2. The feast also refers to the crowd and the influx of pilgrims gathered in Jerusalem for this occasion. The Pharisees feared that Jesus would be arrested "during the feast, so that there would not be a tumult among the people" (Matthew 26:5), showing that the feast attracts a multitude that could react. Similarly, "some Greeks, among those who had come to worship during the feast" (John 12:20) illustrates this convergence of faithful coming from afar.
3. The feast can refer to the moment or period of the celebration: "About the middle of the feast, Jesus went up to the temple" (John 7:14) indicates a specific point in time during the days of festivity. Thus, "going to the feast" or "being at the feast" means participating in this defined period.
4. By extension, fulfilling or observing the feast means participating fully according to custom: "according to the custom of the feast" (Luke 2:42) reminds that each feast has its traditional practices, religious acts, and observances that the faithful must respect.
G1859.origine: The Greek word heortē comes from a root expressing the idea of "fixed moment" or "time of gathering." In Hebrew, it primarily translates chag (literally "to dance, to rejoice"), which designates the three major pilgrimages to the Temple, and also moëd ("appointed time," "set time"), emphasizing the regular and instituted nature of these celebrations. The Hebrew word chag evokes the festive and joyful origin of these gatherings, while moëd highlights the aspect of divinely fixed appointments. Among the Greeks, heortē more broadly designates any feast or festival, religious or civil.
G1859.emploi: The word heortē appears 25 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels (especially John) and Acts, always to designate Jewish feasts. The three feasts most often mentioned are Passover, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and the Feast of Tabernacles. John uses the word intensively during Jesus' ministry in Jerusalem: several passages report that Jesus "went up" to the feast, taught in the temple, and confronted the authorities there (John 7:2, 7:8, 7:10, 7:14, 11:56, 12:12). Luke emphasizes the familial context and piety: Jesus' parents follow the annual custom (Luke 2:41, 2:42). Matthew and Mark note that the Jewish leaders hesitated to arrest Jesus during the feast, for fear of a popular uproar (Matthew 26:5, Mark 14:2), revealing the political and social importance of these gatherings. Acts 18:21 shows that Paul also observed the feasts. Colossians 2:16 mentions them to declare that Christians should no longer be judged on their observance. The word thus designates an essential social, religious, and calendrical framework of Jewish life.
G1859.portee: For the Christian reader, the feast embodies the authentic Jewish context of Jesus and his early disciples. It shows that Jesus participated in the religious life of Israel and addressed the people during moments of spiritual concentration and gathering. It also highlights the tension between the old covenant (prescribed observance) and the new (Colossians 2:16 suggests that these observances no longer bind the Christian). Finally, it reminds us that salvation in Christ was accomplished in the concrete history of a people, with its rhythms, traditions, and places. For Paul, Christian freedom means no longer being subject to judgment regarding these observances, while respecting the conscience of others.

sens: Verbal commitment to fulfill or give something to someone
Thing promised, object or blessing promised
Divine promise, God's commitment to His people
Reality or blessing expected, received as certain
Word given, assurance given to someone
G1860.detail:
1. A promise is primarily the act of saying to someone: "I will give you this" or "This will happen to you." It is a verbal commitment, a pledged word. In Acts 23:21, there is mention of a promise made by conspirators, that is to say, an ordinary human promise.

2. The promise also refers to the very thing that is promised, the gift or the good promised. In 2 Timothy 1:1, Paul speaks of "the promise of life" — he names eternal life itself, which is the object of the divine promise.

3. In the New Testament, the word primarily designates the commitments that God has made to His people and their ancestors. In Acts 26:6, it is "the fulfillment of the promise that God made to our fathers" — the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David. These promises are at the heart of the history of salvation.

4. A promise also becomes that in which one has confidence, what one expects with certainty: in Hebrews 10:36, "what has been promised to you" is presented as something to be obtained, a guaranteed reward. It is the promised blessing transformed into concrete hope.

5. The promise is a word of guarantee: it commits the one who makes it. In 2 Corinthians 1:20, "all the promises of God" are "yes" in Christ — that is to say, confirmed, certain, reliable.
G1860.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb *épangéllo* (to announce beforehand, to promise) formed with the prefix *épi-* (toward, upon) and *angéllo* (to announce, to bear a message). The basic image is that of "announcement": one announces to someone what will be. This root is active in the Bible: the verb *épangéllo* is used to say that God "promises." In Hebrew, the corresponding word is often *dibrou* or words from the root *nidhar* (to vow, to promise), but the idea remains the same: the word of commitment.
G1860.emploi: The word *promise* appears about 50 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and in the epistle to the Hebrews. It is rarely used for purely human promises (Acts 23:21); the vast majority of uses concern God's promises. These promises cover several realities: the promised land (Hebrews 11:9), eternal life (2 Timothy 1:1), the Holy Spirit called "the Spirit of promise" (Ephesians 1:13), the resurrection and the return of Christ (2 Peter 3:4). Paul emphasizes that the promises made to Abraham are fulfilled in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:16-18, Romans 4:13-16). In Hebrews 11, the ancients "saw from afar" the promises (Hebrews 11:13), meaning they believed without seeing them fulfilled. Promises are therefore fundamental: they structure all of God's revelation.
G1860.portee: The promise is at the heart of the relationship between God and His people. Understanding this word means grasping that God is not capricious, but that He commits Himself, that He keeps His word. For the Christian, this means that faith is a trust in God's faithfulness: to believe is to rely on His promises. The promises also call us to perseverance — while waiting for their fulfillment, we are not abandoned, but on the way to what God has guaranteed us in Jesus Christ.

sens: To announce, to proclaim publicly
To solemnly affirm that one will do something
To commit to give or grant something to someone
To declare or confess a conviction, a faith
To guarantee by a promise that something will happen
G1861.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is "to announce" or "to proclaim": to make a news or decision publicly known. It is the idea of making manifest, of going to someone to say.

2. From this comes the main meaning in the New Testament: "to promise," that is to say, to solemnly commit to accomplishing something. When the disciples say to Judas, "we promise you money" (Mark 14:11), they are making a commitment to him.

3. The promise can also pertain to what one will give or grant: it is the idea of assured giving. God promises eternal life (Titus 1:2); someone promises an inheritance (Hebrews 11:11).

4. The word can also mean "to profess" or "to publicly declare one's faith." When a woman "makes a profession of serving God" (1 Timothy 2:10), she openly confesses her attachment to God.

5. Finally, to promise can mean "to guarantee": to affirm with assurance that something will happen. Abraham "was fully convinced that what God promised, He was able to perform" (Romans 4:21).
G1861.origine: The word comes from the prefix ἐπί ("upon, toward") and the verb ἀγγέλλω ("to announce, to report"). The starting image is that of going to someone to announce something solemnly. The promise is therefore an announcement that engages the word and honor of the one who makes it. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often uses this verb to translate אָמַר ("to say") in contexts where God commits Himself to His people.
G1861.emploi: The verb appears 15 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles (Hebrews, James, 1 Timothy, Titus, 2 Peter, 1 John, Romans, Galatians) and in Mark and Acts. Three meanings dominate. First, human promise: Judas promises money (Mark 14:11), the disciples promise an inheritance (Hebrews 11:11). Next, and more frequently, divine promise: God promises eternal life, the Holy Spirit, blessing, and it is on these promises that the believer's faith rests (Hebrews 6:13; Titus 1:2; 1 John 2:25). Finally, the sense of "to profess" or "to declare": confessing one's faith in God (1 Timothy 2:10), professing knowledge of Christ (1 Timothy 6:21). Hebrews often returns to the faithfulness of the One who promised (10:23; 12:26).
G1861.portee: This word reminds the reader that the relationship between God and the believer rests on the given word: God promises, and His promise cannot fail. That is why faith consists of relying on divine promises as on an unshakeable rock. But the word also invites the believer to keep his promises and to openly profess his faith, not in secret, but in actions and words.

sens: solemn commitment to give or do something
that which is assured, expected, hoped for by virtue of that commitment
G1862.detail:
1. A promise is a solemn commitment by which someone obliges themselves to give or do something. It is a weighty word, one can count on. In 2 Peter 1:4, God's great and precious promises engage His faithfulness toward us.
2. The word also designates what is assured to us, what we expect and hope for because God has promised it. In 2 Peter 3:13, the promise of new heavens and a new earth is what Christians await with certainty from the Lord.
G1862.origine: The word comes from the verb épagellô, which means "to announce, to declare solemnly." It is formed from the prefix epi ("toward") and the verb agellô ("to bear a message"). It is therefore the idea of an official announcement, a commitment directed toward someone. The Greek Old Testament used this word to translate the promises that God made to Israel.
G1862.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the second epistle of Peter. In both cases, it refers to God's promises. First, these are the divine promises that allow believers to become partakers of the divine nature. Then, it is the promise of new heavens and a new earth where righteousness will reign. In both uses, the promise expresses what God commits to accomplish for His people, and on which the Christian can base his hope.
G1862.portee: These promises of God addressed to Christians are one of the greatest sources of confidence and joy in the life of faith. They remind us that God does not speak lightly: His commitment holds, even regarding what seems impossible (to become partakers of the divine nature, to see a restored world). They invite the Christian to place his hope, not in the present world marked by corruption, but in the faithful fulfillment of God's word.

sens: To bring something upon someone or a group, to inflict it
To attract a bad consequence, a judgment, or ruin
G1863.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of bringing something — generally a weight, a responsibility, or a consequence — upon someone else. In Acts 5:28, the apostles are accused of wanting to "bring down the blood of this man" upon the leaders, meaning to make them responsible for his death and to burden them with his guilt. It is an image of a weight placed on another's shoulders.
2. The word is also used to describe how someone voluntarily or involuntarily attracts a disaster upon themselves. In 2 Peter 2:1, false teachers "will bring upon themselves swift destruction": their own conduct leads them toward God's judgment. It is less about imposing from the outside than rushing headlong into misfortune oneself.
G1863.origine: The word combines the prefix "epi" ("upon") and the verb "ago" ("to lead, to bring"). The basic image is that of leading something toward someone or bringing it upon them. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew "bo" in the causative form, which means "to bring in" or "to lead in."
G1863.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the context of judgment or responsibility. In Acts 5:28, Peter and John are confronted by the Sanhedrin over the accusation that their teaching brings the blood of a condemned man upon the authorities. In 2 Peter 2:1 and 2:5, the apostle describes how false prophets and the wicked "bring" upon themselves divine judgment — their own behavior becomes the cause of their condemnation. In all cases, the word denotes a process of leading toward an unfortunate outcome.
G1863.portee: This word reminds us of an important moral truth: our actions have consequences that fall upon us or upon those we influence. For the believer, it emphasizes the responsibility of Christian teaching and warns against false teachers whose words divert from God's path. It also invites vigilance: not to attract judgment upon oneself through unfaithfulness.

sens: to fight with all one's strength for a cause
to ardently defend what has been entrusted to us
to resolutely engage in a spiritual struggle
G1864.detail:
1. This verb paints the image of an athlete or a warrior who wholeheartedly engages in a fight. The prefix "epi-" intensifies the idea: one does not fight half-heartedly, but with passion and determination. In Jude 3, the apostle urges believers to "contend for the faith" — not a mere weak defense, but a resolute commitment, as one throws oneself into the arena.
2. The word emphasizes less the final victory than the effort itself, the self-giving in the struggle. This is why Jude uses it for the faith entrusted to the saints: it is not about defeating an external enemy in a decisive battle, but about persevering tirelessly in the defense of what has been entrusted to us and that we must pass on.
G1864.origine: The verb is formed from the prefix "epi-" ("upon," "against") and "agōnizomai" (to struggle, to fight), which comes from the noun "agōn" (the struggle, the fight, the arena). The basic image is that of the Greek athlete engaged in competition. The noun "agōnia" (agony, extreme anguish) shares the same root and reflects the intense tension of the fight.
G1864.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 3. Jude uses it to urge persecuted or threatened believers by false teachers to defend the authentic faith. The use of the word suggests that this defense is not a mere theological debate, but an existential struggle where the stakes are the salvation and purity of the faith received from the apostles. It is a call to mobilize the whole person for a cause that transcends them.
G1864.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites examination of one's own commitment to the faith. It is not enough to be passive or indifferent to lies; one is called to contend for the truth with the same fervor as an athlete or a warrior. This call to vigilance and determination aligns with the awareness that spiritual life demands a continual struggle and active faithfulness.

sens: To assemble in large numbers, to form a compact crowd
(Figuratively) To accumulate, to concentrate in one place
G1865.detail:
1. The word describes a spontaneous gathering of people pressing together. In Luke 11:29, the crowd gathers around Jesus to see and hear him: thousands of people concentrate in the same place, drawn by his presence. It is the movement of convergence of many people toward a central point.
2. The figurative sense extends this image: things (people, events, intentions) accumulate and concentrate together, like the people in the Gospel. The idea is always one of a compact and visible accumulation.
G1865.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "epi" (upon, near) and the root "athroizo" (to assemble, to gather). This root evokes the action of grouping dispersed elements together. The passive form (to gather together) emphasizes that the crowd gathers spontaneously, as if pushed by a force acting upon it.
G1865.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in the passage of Luke 11:29. Luke uses it to describe the moment when a large crowd presses around Jesus, seeking a sign. The context is one of a growing gathering: people arrive from everywhere, adding themselves to one another, until forming a compact group. The verb emphasizes the massive and almost overwhelming character of this human concentration.
G1865.portee: This word reminds us of the power of attraction exerted by Jesus: his presence is enough to mobilize the crowds, to make them converge. But in this passage, Luke also highlights Jesus' concern over this curious and unbelieving crowd. The gathering of bodies often reflects a sincere quest, but it can also mask a purely spectacular quest for the miracle. The reader is invited to examine their own desire: do they approach Jesus out of curiosity or true faith?

sens: Christian from Rome in the first century
G1866.detail: Epainète is a believer who lived in Rome during the time of the apostle Paul. Paul affectionately greets him, calling him "my beloved" and gives him a special honor: he was "the firstfruits of Asia for Christ" (Romans 16:5), meaning the first convert to faith in Jesus in the region of Asia Minor. He is an example of those forgotten witnesses of early Christianity that Paul sought to honor publicly in his letter.
G1866.origine: The name Epainète comes from Greek and literally means "worthy of praise" or "to be congratulated" (from "epainō", to praise). It is a Greek name borne by a believer whose personal story fully justified this meaning: the first convert in his region, he embodied a reason for rejoicing in the nascent Church.
G1866.emploi: Epainète appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:5, where Paul lists the Christians he greets. This brief but warm mention reveals the importance Paul placed on recognizing the pioneers and faithful of the Church. By calling him "the firstfruits of Asia," Paul emphasizes that Epainète was the first fruit of the Gospel in that region, before missionary work expanded widely there.
G1866.portee: Epainète embodies the ordinary believer whose conversion opened the door for others. His story reminds us that in God's plan, every first conversion in a place or region holds immense value: it becomes the mustard seed from which the tree of the Kingdom springs. Paul explicitly honors this forgotten disciple, teaching us that God does not lose sight of any soul and that faithful work in silence, known only to the apostle, deserves recognition.

sens: Express approval, admiration towards someone or something
Recognize and celebrate the qualities, commendable actions of someone
Formally approve a behavior, a way of acting
G1867.detail: 1. To praise means to express approval towards a person or an action. It is to acknowledge that something or someone has acted well. In Luke 16:8, the master praises the dishonest steward for his shrewdness, even though the act itself is blameworthy. 2. To praise also means to publicly celebrate the qualities and merits of someone. Paul rejoices in praising the Corinthians for their obedience to his teachings (1 Corinthians 11:2). 3. Conversely, to refuse to praise is to express disapproval. Paul refuses to praise the Corinthians who gather in a disorderly and unloving manner: their assembly becomes worse instead of improving (1 Corinthians 11:17 and 11:22).
G1867.origine: The Greek word ἐπαινέω comes from two elements: ἐπί (epi, "upon") and αἰνέω (aineō, "to speak"). It thus evokes the idea of speaking "upon" someone, that is, well of them. In Hebrew, this verb primarily translates to הָלַל (hāllal, root of "Hallelujah") and שָׁבַח (šābhaḥ), both expressing praise. It is a rich word: to praise someone is also to give them value through our words.
G1867.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's letters. Paul uses it to express his approval of the Corinthians when they obey (1 Corinthians 11:2), but refuses to praise them when they disobey or act wrongly (1 Corinthians 11:17, 11:22). Significantly, it is not a common verb: its rarity underscores that the context of praise or approval is important. The word can be constructed in several ways: with an accusative (to praise someone directly), or with a conjunction (to praise someone for what..., that is, by giving the reason). Words of approval carry weight.
G1867.portee: Praise and approval shape the life of the church. Paul uses this verb to encourage spiritual growth: praising what is good reinforces good actions, while refusing to praise disorder and selfishness helps the assembly to correct itself. It is a call to Christians to discern what deserves approval and to build the church through righteous words.

sens: Expression of gratitude and admiration towards someone
Favorable judgment, approval
Honor and glory given to God
G1868.detail:
1. Praise is primarily the expression of gratitude and admiration directed towards someone for what they have done or who they are. It is the sincere compliment we give them: in Romans 13:3, the one who does good receives the approval of authority, their public esteem. In 2 Corinthians 8:18, a brother has built a good reputation, his praise (what is said well of him) has spread among the churches.
2. Praise can also be a positive evaluation, a favorable judgment rendered on a person or their actions. In 1 Corinthians 4:5, each will receive from God the praise that is due to them — that is, the just appreciation of what they have truly been worth.
3. In the highest sense, praise is the honor and glory we give to God for who He is and what He does. Ephesians 1:6 speaks of serving "to the praise of the glory of His grace." It is the cry of a grateful heart that rises to the Lord.
G1868.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to speak well of," "to commend." It is formed from elements that express the idea of approving and honoring. In Hebrew, the equivalent is often found in the word תְּהִלָּה (praise, song), which denotes the action of celebrating God. The Greek word ἔπαινος refers to both mutual praise among humans and the worship given to God.
G1868.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, almost always in the epistles. It first denotes human praise — the esteem one gains through their actions (Romans 13:3, 2 Corinthians 8:18) or the final appreciation that God will have for each (1 Corinthians 4:5). But its major use is the praise directed to God: it is the joyful response of creation to divine grace (Ephesians 1:6, 1:12), the expression of grateful faith (Philippians 1:11, 4:8), and the fruit of our sanctification (1 Peter 1:7, 2:14). Romans 2:29 provides the spiritual definition: true praise does not come from human approval, but from God alone.
G1868.portee: Understanding the word praise means grasping that our lives must bear fruit for the glory of God. It also means understanding that true approval does not come from men, but from God alone, and that it is this divine approval that matters. Living for the praise of God transforms our priorities: what guides us is no longer reputation or judgment from others, but the recognition of what God has done for us in Christ.

sens: Raise a part of the body upwards
Raise the voice to speak loudly
Remove, take away
Swell with pride, become arrogant
G1869.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to raise the eyes, hands, head. Jesus "raised His eyes" before multiplying the loaves (John 6:5), and Peter "raised his voice" to proclaim the message at Pentecost (Acts 2:14). It is a simple, physical gesture, often linked to attention or the intention to speak with authority.
2. To raise the voice means to shout, to speak with force and solemnity: the Jews "raised their voices" against Paul (Acts 22:22). It is to raise the tone to be heard or to express a strong emotion.
3. In the sense of removing or taking away: the rich man in hell "raised his heel" against Lazarus (John 13:18), meaning he struck or opposed him with disdain. This expresses a hostile action or a gesture of rejection.
4. Figuratively, "to be raised" with pride or arrogance means to swell with vanity (2 Corinthians 10:5, 11:20). Pride "lifts you up," making you arrogant and pretentious.
G1869.origine: The word combines the preposition "epi" (upon, over) and the root "aïrô" (to raise, to take away). It literally means "to raise upwards." In Hebrew, the main word translated is "nassâ" (נָשָׂא), which has the same physical and figurative meaning: it primarily means to raise, but also to carry, support, and even to forgive. This Hebrew-Greek root suggests the idea of movement upwards, dignity, and authority.
G1869.emploi: The verb appears 19 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Acts. Luke uses it very often: to raise the eyes (Luke 6:20, 16:23, 18:13) and the hands (Luke 24:50). John also uses this verb for gestures of Jesus before miracles (John 4:35, 6:5, 17:1) or symbolic acts (John 13:18). In Acts, it is mostly "to raise the voice": Peter at Pentecost (2:14), the crowd against Paul (14:11, 22:22). Only once does it refer to a ship's sail (Acts 27:40). Figuratively, Paul uses it to speak of pride that "rises up" against God (2 Corinthians 10:5, 11:20). The word can also express a hostile action or disdain: to raise the heel against someone (John 13:18).
G1869.portee: This word reveals how the Bible links bodily gestures to the intention of the heart. When Jesus "raises His eyes" to heaven, it is not a simple movement: it is an act of trust towards the Father. When Peter "raises his voice," it is an act of courage and faith. Conversely, when pride "rises up" in us, it is a danger: it is to forget that only God should be "lifted up." This verb calls the believer to examine their gestures and words: do they truly lift towards God, or towards oneself?

sens: to feel shame, embarrassment, or dishonor in the face of something or someone
to refuse to acknowledge or support someone out of fear of judgment or ridicule
to regret past actions and feel confusion about them
G1870.detail:
1. To be ashamed is to feel a deep discomfort, an embarrassment that makes you lower your eyes. It is to experience dishonor in front of a situation or a person. Paul declares: "I am not ashamed of the Gospel" (Romans 1:16), which means he does not feel the discomfort or embarrassment that others might feel when talking about faith.
2. To be ashamed of someone also means to reject them or refuse to acknowledge them publicly, out of fear of others' judgment. Jesus says: "Whoever is ashamed of me and my words... the Son of Man will also be ashamed of them" (Mark 8:38), meaning that openly rejecting Him brings divine judgment in return.
3. To be ashamed also means to look back on one's actions with regret and confusion: "What fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed?" (Romans 6:21) — it is to contemplate one's past with disgust and contrition.
G1870.origine: The word combines the prefix "epi" (upon, towards) with the verb "to be ashamed." This composition intensifies the idea: shame is not just present, it takes hold of you, it weighs upon you. In Hebrew, related words (like "bûsh") also express this reaction of the body and heart: the redness of the cheeks, the lowering of the gaze, the feeling of unworthiness.
G1870.emploi: This verb appears nine times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in the Gospels. Jesus uses it to warn His disciples: being ashamed of Him on earth will have eternal consequences (Mark 8:38, Luke 9:26). Paul uses it to express his assurance: he is not ashamed of the message he preaches despite persecutions (Romans 1:16, 2 Timothy 1:8 and 1:12). The Epistle to the Hebrews uses it to show that the Son of God is not ashamed to call His believers brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The word can also express regret for past sinful actions (Romans 6:21). Throughout the New Testament, it questions the relationship between public faithfulness to Jesus and future judgment.
G1870.portee: This word highlights an internal Christian struggle: the courage to confess one's faith in the face of the world. It calls the believer not to sacrifice the honor of Jesus Christ to human fear, for rejecting Jesus has eternal implications. It also invites repentance: looking at one's past with shame is to turn sincerely towards God. It is a word that awakens the conscience and strengthens resolve.

sens: to beg, to live by asking for one's bread
to implore, to humbly and urgently plead with someone
G1871.detail:
